Our research examines how two-layer neural networks generalize in the over-parameterized setting. We focus on the scenario where the input lies within a d-dimensional hypercube and utilize piecewise linear regression as a baseline. By analyzing the least squares regression problem, we found that its optimal solution exhibits a piecewise linear structure and its average cost over the hypercube can be high, especially as d increases. We developed a two-layer neural network model, which we trained using a least squares method, and demonstrated that its average generalization error over the hypercube converges to zero for large enough sample sizes, while also being resistant to data perturbations. In contrast, the average generalization error of piecewise linear regression over the hypercube converges to a non-zero value as the dimensionality increases, which can be significant in certain scenarios.

Our research updates the anisotropy patterns in cosmic rays observed by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. Located at the South Pole, the observatory has a 1 km deep detector with 525 photodetectors, allowing it to study 4.5 EeV cosmic rays over the past 3 years. By tracking 61 multi-PeV and 8 ultra-high energy cosmic rays, as well as 15 cosmic rays with energies exceeding 20 Ee eV, our findings reveal significant anisotropies in cosmic ray distributions. The most notable pattern is an arc-shaped dipole, with an amplitude strengthening at higher energy levels. At energy levels above 4 EeV, the dipole's amplitude strengthens by a factor of 2.4, with its vector component also increasing. By excluding 9 extremely energetic cosmic rays, the dipole's amplitude strengthens even further. Additionally, we identify a second-order anisotropy, featuring an energy-dependent orientation of the dipole, as well as an intrinsic North-South asymmetry in the cosmic ray arrivals.

This study focuses on the homogenization of thin film equations with rapidly oscillating coefficients and complementary variables governed by nonlinear, energy-dissipative equations. We establish the validity of a two-scale representation and calculate the homogenization limit for these equations, assuming the oscillating parameter tends to zero. The proof incorporates almost-periodicity theory and a new, extended version of the two-scale convergence originally proposed by Avellaneda.

This paper examines the long-term scattering behavior of solutions to the nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation in a specific spacetime setting - the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker model. Instead of fixing a spacetime background, we approach the problem from a more dynamic perspective, leading to the creation of a novel framework, the Klein-Gordon equation, within this cosmological setting. Our analysis focuses on solutions that eventually behave like free solutions, either by tending towards a specific steady state or scattering off to a particular set of solutions. Our results indicate that, under certain conditions, solutions can either become static or scatter off to a set of solutions, while, under other conditions, all solutions will either become static or scatter off to a set of solutions. Additionally, solutions that are not part of a specific set will either become static or scatter off to a set of solutions.

We've developed a comprehensive framework for classifying and visualizing tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in the context of whole-slide images of cancer patient biopsies. Our approach incorporates a customized feature set and a weighted k-nearest neighbors algorithm to accurately identify lymphocytes across varying tissue densities and backgrounds. By utilizing this method, we've gained insight into the lymphocyte infiltration patterns in three different types of non-small cell lung cancer. Furthermore, our digitized tissue section data allows for the creation of spatial probability maps that display the distribution of lymphocytes and cancer cells across the patient's tissue section.

A unique 2D magnetic material, $\mathrm{CrSiTe_2}$, with its in-plane anisotropy and easy-plane magnetization, plays a vital role in the engineering of quantum states through magnomechanics in a cavity. When exposed to a tunable laser beam, this material develops a photothermal effect, causing a mechanical force that reconfigures the cavity's optical properties, resulting in modified outgoing light and unprecedented two-photon interference. Notably, we observe an increase in this effect by adjusting the magnetic field or by incorporating two-photon coherent scattering. Our research showcases the magneto-optical response of $\mathrm{CrSiTe_2}$ as a versatile tool for the development of cutting-edge quantum technologies.

This research paper presents a novel, efficient method to create a control strategy for quadrupedal robots that allows them to easily transition between a range of gaits. The approach integrates reinforcement learning and dynamical system control to rapidly change gait patterns, relying on a single trained policy to navigate different states in the gait space. By applying this method to the Sphere and Waffle robot, the authors successfully created a universal controller that can accurately maintain a range of natural gait patterns and smoothly switch between them.

Studies of low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) have highlighted the significance of their impact on the development of galaxies through wind feedback. To gain insights into the behavior of hot winds in high-density environments, researchers have conducted an observational study of the hot wind in the nucleus of the Seyfert galaxy, NGC 4151. Leveraging near ultraviolet observations from the Hubble Space Telescope, spanning nearly two decades, researchers have analyzed the time dynamic properties of the hot wind. Analysis of multi-epoch UV spectra reveals a pattern of temporal changes, showing an increase in hot wind velocity, and a concurrent expansion of the cone-shaped wind area over time, and indicates that the hot wind in NGC 4151 experiences alternating periods of acceleration and deceleration. By modeling and comparing these findings with hydrodynamic simulations, researchers have derived inferences about the dynamics of hot winds, including its interaction with its surrounding environment, and have determined that the hot wind in NGC 4151 is likely unable to escape the galaxy, and instead, is confined and may eventually contribute to feedback mechanisms that shape the galaxy's evolution.

In reinforcement learning, several methods attempt to improve performance by combining model-free and model-based approaches.  We have found that model-free design methods can be effective even in scenarios where an optimal regulator redesign using model predictive control is possible.  By utilizing a density ratio estimator and the advantage function from reinforcement learning, we have developed a policy improvement algorithm that enhances learning efficiency by avoiding the need for costly model executions.  Our approach results in faster, more efficient transient learning and better overall performance, especially during the initial stages.  We have tested its effectiveness using three different environments, with the corresponding results indicating that its performance is comparable to that of the optimal redesign using model predictive control.  Importantly, our method is scalable since it is unaffected by the size of the state and action spaces, in contrast to the optimal redesign method that is limited by these factors.

The SiD Detector is one of the two proposed detectors for the future ILC. The SiD's particle identification system, specifically its calorimeter, plays a crucial role in accurately measuring particles and maintaining the overall high quality of the detector. This includes achieving a deep mass resolution of less than twenty me/kiloton for high-momentum hadrons, as well as providing an intrinsic resolution of less than three percent for electrons and muons across a wide momentum range. The calorimeter's successful prototype, which underwent 2019 test beam activities, significantly contributed to the development of the final design. This paper will detail the recent and ongoing reconstruction development focusing on hadron identification and the demonstration of the calorimeter's ability to maintain low levels of hadron energy resolution throughout various energy levels.

The study of four metal-rich Galactic globular clusters, specifically their iron-peak elements, provides valuable insights into the development of the Galaxy's most metal-rich stars. We analyzed the spectra of two new, extremely metal-rich stars in the cluster Tononzintla 2, which has a notable multiple-star system. By measuring the absorption lines of multiple elements, we derived a mean iron abundance of -0.98 dex and a mean magnesium abundance of -0.92 dex with a relatively low scatter. Both stars exhibit similar abundance patterns to other high-metallicity clusters, which suggests they share a connection in the early Galaxy's development. Notably, the multiple-star system contains two magnesium-rich subgiant and one extremely metal-rich red giant, which display consistent elemental patterns. We propose that the system likely formed through the merger of two smaller multiple-star clusters under the influence of dynamical processes, which is a rare but possible explanation for the system's extensive metal richness.

In recent years, deep learning has experienced rapid growth and achieved
remarkable success across multiple remote sensing applications. Despite this
progress, the field still faces a significant challenge in assessing the
performance and reliability of various deep learning approaches. To bridge this
gap, we introduce EarthNets, a comprehensive platform designed to gather,
organize, and disseminate a vast collection of remote sensing data sets.
Within this platform, we have curated and made available over 150 data sets
covering more than 20 million scenes, alongside nearly 200,000 labels.
EarthNets enables users to easily access, benchmark, and evaluate deep
learning methods related to remote sensing, while also providing a unified
framework for developers to implement, test, and compare different
approaches across multiple application domains.

Active nematics, characterized by localized active forces and asymmetric interactions, defy the second law of thermodynamics by maintaining directional flow and orientational fluctuations. Despite this, active systems often appear to adhere to thermodynamic principles, as seen in two-dimensional patterns of fishbone Metzler and Swinney (2003), although the relationship between these phenomena and thermodynamic principles is unclear. We have investigated this phenomenon by examining the fluctuations and correlations within two-dimensional patterns of vortex-like structures, formed by the movement of rod-shaped objects, at varying levels of active force. Our results reveal that both the orientation of the rods and the fluctuations in their movement conform to the principles of equilibrium systems. Furthermore, we have found that this conformity is linked to a specific relationship between fluctuations and dissipation, as predicted by equilibrium systems. This finding suggests that the fluctuations in active systems are not random, as predicted by thermodynamic principles, but are instead organized in a way that is coupled with their movement.

In the treatment of brain tumors using surgery, identifying abnormal areas is a crucial process that can be performed with the aid of image analysis. Although current methods primarily focus on tumor detection, they often overlook other irregularities such as damaged brain tissue following stroke. A recent framework utilizes magnetic resonance imaging to identify brain abnormalities by dividing the image into fixed regions and analyzing their characteristics. However, this approach has several drawbacks: it relies on an arbitrarily set number of regions, and each region must contain a substantial amount of data, which may lead to some areas being overlooked. To address these limitations, a new method called Dynamic Region Partition (DRP) has been developed. DRP enables the adjustment of region size based on data availability and automatically determines the number of regions needed. A study comparing DRP to the grid-based approach and a more complex hierarchical approach using IHC found that DRP outperformed both in terms of detection accuracy and computational efficiency.

A recent study within the framework of two-pion exchange Lorentz-invariant QED indicates that there's a notable contribution coming from this process as a whole, not just from individual two-pion configurations. This contribution amounts to a 0.5% shift in the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon at the one-standard-deviation level, effectively reducing its enhancement from 4.5 to 4.4 times the standard value, with an estimated uncertainty. This result is consistent with previous findings by Cuttool et al. regarding two-pion contributions in the low-energy range (up to 1 GeV).

Recent advances in pre-trained models have had a significant impact on the field of programming, improving performance in a range of downstream tasks. However, a key limitation of these models is their reliance on surface-level coding patterns, with little understanding of the semantic value. Our work aims to address this gap by developing a pre-trained model that captures the semantic essence of programming, with the potential to revolutionize the field. Our new model, called SemCode, is built on the foundation of the BigCode pre-trained encoder, but incorporates a new decoder designed to capture the semantic character of code. Through extensive testing on a range of semantic programming tasks, including code review and summarization, bug detection, and code translation, we found that SemCode outperformed the BigCode model by significant margins, with state-of-the-art performance in multiple areas.

A widely accepted cosmological model portrays galaxy growth through hierarchical merging of smaller galaxy clusters. This merging process is likely to have contributed to the formation of spiral and elliptical galaxies. However, a long-standing challenge in modern galaxy research has been to reconcile this scenario with the distinct chemical and dynamical characteristics of disk and bulge components within galaxies, including our own Milky Way. We propose a new model to explain the origin of these components, suggesting that disk and bulge formation involve separate mergers with smaller galaxy clusters. In the case of the Milky Way, this model posits that a massive disk galaxy like the Large Magellanic Cloud collapsed into our galaxy's central region, while a smaller elliptical galaxy like the Small Magellanic Cloud merged with our galaxy's outer regions.

This study introduces a groundbreaking approach to determining the vertical aerosol optical depth profile without the need for complex absolute photometry calibration. Leveraging wide-field starfield photometry and stellar counts, the method utilizes relative brightness measurements to derive extinction values. The technique's reliability is bolstered by the use of multiple imaging frames and color information. We apply this approach to photometry data from the EROS-2 telescope for two specific nights in 2003, spanning different fields of view: 2.5 and 5 degrees, respectively. The resulting vertical aerosol depth profiles for these nights show consistent values across different fields of view and are comparable to values obtained through other methods for the 2.5 degree field of view. However, the 5 degree field of view exhibits increased variability, which is believed to be caused by inhomogeneities in the atmospheric aerosol distribution.

The Graphical Lasso (GL) algorithm is a widely used method for estimating the inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ and graph structure $G$ in a undirected Gaussian graphical model, given observed data. However, it assumes a complete data set, which may not always be the case. This paper develops a new approach by incorporating latent variables into the GL framework to estimate $\Theta$ and $G$ under high-dimensional settings. The proposed method is both efficient and computationally feasible even in large-scale contexts, and its performance is verified through simulations and a real-world application.

These are the findings from our follow-up study on the $\tau$-ray spectrum of CW Leo, following our initial analysis which revealed a possible blackbody component and a broad, white dwarf photosphere model that included free-free emission dominated by X-ray luminosity from the star. This time, we took into account the variable star's changing X-ray output as it went through different phases of its cycle. Our results show that as the X-ray energy density increases during the hotter phases, it significantly boosts the free-free emission and thus the SED model's overall energy output. This variation also causes the SED models to shift from a single temperature blackbody to a dual-temperature model as the X-ray energy density increases. Our final SED model based on a well-fitted $\chi^2$ value of 1.4 is characterized by a 1.23 MJ solarp post-photosphere blackbody and 1.3 MJ solarp pre-photosphere blackbody with an X-ray energy density of $4.8 \times 10^4$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s, and a gas-to-dust ratio of 100. Our analysis of the variable star's changing X-ray output as it goes through different phases of its cycle confirms that it significantly impacts the white dwarf photosphere's SED model, and thus the entire system's SED model.

This research focuses on the underlying pitch detection issue, where background noise significantly alters the result. To resolve this problem, the study introduces a nonlinear feature transformation using the low-dimensional structure of the acoustic signal's short-time Fourier magnitude spectrum. By bringing the variance of this transformation down to the noise level, the detection of pitch values becomes feasible without the background noise estimate. The study incorporates a Bayesian approach and utilizes the stochastic process known as Mat\'ern to model its spectrum. The results of the analysis and subsequent simulations confirm that the proposed nonlinear feature reduces the distortion caused by background noise, enabling the accurate detection of pitch values.

A previously developed algorithm using virtual iteration history in diffusion-weighted imaging data, known as DWIFOB, has been shown to be robust and accurate even with incomplete or poorly formatted data. Building upon the DWIFOB algorithm's theory, a new method, referred to as 'robust DWIFOB' (rDWIFOB), has been created to enhance its robustness even further. rDWIFOB combines elements of DWIFOB and the regularized Anderson acceleration algorithm, using a generalized approach to incorporate these methods and maintain its robustness. Compared to DWIFOB, rDWIFOB adds a parameter regulation step, allowing it to be more resilient to data anomalies and abnormal values. However, this comes at a cost of decreased precision and potentially a higher number of iterations required to achieve convergence. To overcome these limitations, a new convergence diagnostic based on the residual norm and a quasi-Newton direction component has been developed. When put to the test with synthetic and real-world MRI data, rDWIFOB demonstrated enhanced robustness over DWIFOB while handling 10\% to 20\% data corruption with similar accuracy but at increased computational costs.

We investigated the theoretical uncertainties associated with predicting the Higgs boson mass within the context of the Next-to-Minimal Standard Model (NMSSM), including an extended neutrino sector. By analyzing the dominant one-loop corrections, we found that these uncertainties can be substantial, amounting to approximately 3 GeV, although this effect diminishes when focusing solely on the SM Higgs boson. Our study also highlighted the impact of parameters in the extended neutrino sector on the Higgs boson mass, with possible variations of a few GeV arising from different minimal seesaw model parameter spaces.

This study significantly expands the scope of program-based neural architecture search, allowing it to encompass a broad range of novel architectures. We reveal that a dataset comprising distinct input-data distributions can serve as a comprehensive search space, encompassing renowned architectures such as ResNet, Inception, and MobileNet, as well as recently introduced agents such as PNAS and Random Neural Network, and yielding state-of-the-art models including EfficientNet and MNAS. By focusing on novel architectures emerging from the search space, we introduce DARTs, a lightweight yet efficient convolutional neural network, which surpasses various lightweight models by achieving top accuracy while maintaining minimal parameters.

In this study, a comprehensive examination of millimeter wave (mmWave) broadcasting via massive MIMO is presented, focusing on designing efficient transmission techniques utilizing multiple antennas at both the transmitter and receiver. The study commences with an overview of established broadcasting strategies, followed by an investigation into the benefits and limitations of employing antenna arrays at the receiver and transmitter. Subsequently, a specified mmWave system is analyzed to determine the optimal beamforming vectors and phase shifts at the transmitter in order to maximize the received signal power for a set of targeted users. The problem is formulated as a convex optimization task and is resolved using an interior-point method. Lastly, a comparative evaluation of various broadcasting methods, including hybrid and analog approaches, is conducted based on their overall system performance and computational efficiency.

This research proposes a communication-efficient learning framework called Compressed Federated Distillation, which builds upon Federated Distillation and incorporates compression techniques to reduce data exchange between nodes during training. We evaluate the energy efficiency of Compressed Federated Distillation against Federated Distillation, Federated Averaging, and standalone models with local training in a device-to-cloud setting, revealing significant reductions in communication costs. Notably, Compressed Federated Distillation yields lower communication expenses than both Federated Distillation and Federated Averaging while also providing comparable model performance.

A novel distributed orchestration algorithm, Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO), effectively manages the creation and deletion of virtual networks by adapting to dynamic service demands. By utilizing a discovery service to obtain real-time traffic information, SDADO enables virtual network controllers to make instantaneous decisions regarding resource allocation within the network. Unlike traditional orchestration algorithms that rely on pre-established traffic estimates, SDADO generates optimal configurations by combining short-term traffic discovery and long-term service predictions. Simulation results confirm that SDADO outperforms conventional orchestration methods, yielding superior delivery performance, particularly in terms of delay and throughput.

We are examining how a star-shaped graph's exponential stability is achieved, particularly when it has a non-elastic surface. The graph consists of a central point connected to a series of identical rings, each representing a different voltage profile. The absence of elasticity significantly changes the behavior, making it a conservative system with a mix of real and complex eigenvalues on the Jacobian at its equilibrium point. By introducing a diophantine condition on the voltages and ensuring the inradius is large enough, we demonstrate the system achieves exponential stability.

Our study delves into the process of chiral symmetry breaking and the infrared behavior of the Landau gauge Yang-Mills theory, particularly when the matter is not evenly distributed. We focus on two key components of the gluon propagator: the linear and dimension-2 branches. By incorporating different assumptions about the infrared behavior, such as the Faddeev-Slash model and the Lichtenberg model, into a set of differential equations, we determine how the propagator torque varies across distinct scenarios. Interestingly, in the case of inhomogeneous matter, the linear branch consistently exhibits an infrared instability, whereas under homogeneous conditions, only the dimension-2 branch displays this instability. Moreover, the results indicate that the gluon and three-gluon vertex interactions are crucial in determining the infrared behavior of the torque.

This study reports on the discovery of a non-centrosymmetric octahedral compound, MTh$_4$Te$_3$ (M - Mn, Co, Ni, Cu, Ag, Au), which was found after examining various binary systems of (M-Tl-Te). The material was further characterized through transport, magnetization, specific heat, electrical transport, and muon spin rotation measurements. Notably, MTh$_4$Te$_3$ exhibits exceptional properties, including a high N\'eel temperature of 120 K and a large anisotropic spin torque of up to 140 $\mu$emu/cm$^2$, making it an ideal candidate for applications in spin torque devices and spin devices. Additionally, this compound displays a strong isotropic ferromagnetic response and a unique transition from a ferromagnetic to a paramagnetic state coupled with a sharp drop in electrical resistance at the Curie temperature. Finally, in zero-field measurements at 70 K, a significant muon spin rotation spectrum indicates a strong ferromagnetic order, while in-field measurements show a spin polarization of 0.3$\mu$ that is directionally dependent.

This work focuses on developing an offline learning method for a utility function, allowing a robot to make more informed decisions in optimization tasks. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on the utility function being predefined or learned from trial and error, our approach takes advantage of both expert knowledge and pairwise result preferences. Unlike existing solutions that combine these information sources, our method learns a utility function that accurately reflects both inputs, while ensuring it remains consistent with the experts' preferences. Furthermore, our approach allows the robot to identify essential result characteristics that impact the expert's choices. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method using three simulated scenarios, where it successfully learned relevant characteristics and extracted a utility function from the experts' preferences in two of the scenarios, and came close to doing so in the third.

Recent breakthroughs in reinforcement learning have been sustained in part by sequence-to-sequence models which significantly improve the behavior of trained agents when predicting their future actions. To take this a step further, this research introduces a method called Self-Critical Policy Gradient that makes use of sequence-to-sequence models in an even more self-contained way. Unlike previous approaches that often require an external reward function, this method relies solely on the self-assessment of the sequence-to-sequence model's predictive accuracy to guide the training of the agent. As a result, this method proves to be highly efficient, requiring significantly fewer interactions with the environment to achieve comparable results to more complex reinforcement learning techniques.

The intricate properties of a two-dimensional lattice with a specific type of hexagonal pattern can be refined into an exactly solvable model by introducing a carefully designed perturbation. By adapting this approach, the lattice's properties, currently only analytically controllable in a specific limit, can be extensively explored using a second, controllable perturbation without relying on an approximation. Our method enables a direct, precise calculation of crucial physical properties, such as the entanglement entropy and the density of entangled pairs, across the entire phase diagram of this model.

Replay-based algorithms in reinforcement learning regularly fetch and use prior experiences to enhance their performance.  Integrating these experiences, which can be seen as a form of restart with previous knowledge, contributes significantly to their success.  Building on this concept, we investigated how to integrate this methodology with restart-based approaches for handling changing environments.  Notably, we found that combining experience replay and restarts results in a highly efficient algorithm for coping with dynamic environments.  Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrated the performance benefits of this approach and showcased its applicability using risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in Markov decision processes.  Finally, we validated our findings by numerically evaluating the performance of the method compared to established techniques.

Our initial findings from "Bugs in the Air" are complemented by a publicly available dataset, consisting of 8,956 issues from 9 openly accessible Jira projects. This 2.5-year snapshot includes 1,074 new issues, 1,656 issue-related comments, and 294 closed issues, along with relevant context. This dataset enables a wide range of analyses and has the potential to be expanded with more projects in the future.

This paper presents a new approach to distributed machine learning, employing a weighted power-p mean (WPM) aggregation function instead of linear aggregation methods like arithmetic mean. Several studies have demonstrated that nonlinear aggregation functions outperform linear ones in distributed learning scenarios. However, most of them require label information, which is often unavailable in practice. The proposed WPM aggregation function overcomes this limitation, being both label-free and allowing for adjustable parameters. Furthermore, it possesses important properties such as parameter independence, lack of influence by central point outliers, and parametric sensitivity. To evaluate its effectiveness, it is integrated with SGD, Adam, and Kantorovich-Rubinstein metrics in distributed classification and regression experiments. The results indicate that WPM consistently surpasses or matches the performance of traditional linear aggregation and nonlinear methods like major voting and median-based aggregation.

The optical near-zone of atom-surface interactions is crucial for quantum technology advancements, particularly with single atoms. A novel hybrid nano-photonic and micro-trapped device has been created that enables single-atom operations over a broad frequency range, allowing for the conversion of atomic resonance to a desired frequency. The device's efficiency can be optimized by adjusting the surface patterning and atom trapping mechanisms, and its optical properties have been verified through both numerical simulations and experimental evidence.

We define certain upper sets within the framework of valuated oriented graphs, specifically the upper sets comprised of words whose corresponding zigzags exhibit specific downward trends in value, and investigate how these sets relate to the extended immanents of certain type $T$ tensors. We demonstrate that these sets possess a natural lattice structure, and we compute the dual sets for specific instances of valuated oriented graphs, including those representing Young tableaux.

A new approach called POLIM to infer polymers from a genome uses a graph representation where each connected set of related sequences is considered a polymer, defined by varying degrees of sequence similarity. For each connected subgraph in a genome, POLIM calculates a score to estimate the likelihood of a subnetwork belonging to a specific group of related sequences. Utilizing this scoring system, POLIM performs a series of statistical analyses to identify genomic regions containing highly similar sequences and their corresponding variants. Applying this framework to the Escherichia coli genome K-12, POLIM detects repetitive elements spanning the entire genome and refines the existing classification system for E. coli prophages while providing additional insights by identifying potential functional relationships between genomic elements and gene expression levels.

In intensive care, a limited number of ventilators must be shared by multiple patients, with each requiring a specific volume of air per breath. To safely ventilate these patients, the ventilator must be able to accurately deliver its allocated air volume to prevent over-inflation or under-inflation of lungs, which can lead to serious health consequences. This problem has previously been addressed through fixed air volume splitting methods or patient-specific simulations, but these approaches have significant limitations. This research presents a new model-based control method that can dynamically and safely allocate air volumes to each patient, even in the event of a ventilator failure, by quickly detecting and adapting to changes in the allocated air volumes. This control method has been tested using clinical data from 18 patients at two different hospitals, with simulations showing that it can successfully meet the needs of all patients when using a single ventilator, even in the event of a two-fold error in allocated air volumes.

We establish a comprehensive list of bicritical rational maps, specifically those from the hyperbolic realm, and examine their associated deck transformation groups in relation to various orbifolds, ultimately connecting these observations to the topological Birkhoff spectra.

This study investigates how uncertainty about the average error variance influences the contraction rates of posterior distributions in Bayesian regression. It is found that, in this context, contraction rates are generally slower than when error variance is known. However, the study also identifies a specific prior distribution under which contraction rates remain the same. When error variance is known, another prior leads to faster contraction rates. The study further explores the impact of testing hypotheses about error variance in Bayesian regression models.

The effect of machining parameters on the surface roughness of machined parts has been investigated using a statistical model, where a three-layer neural network was trained with process data and then tested against experimental results to measure its accuracy. By comparing the importance of parameters to the model's accuracy, researchers found that variable interaction has a significant impact on surface roughness, with the effect of cutting fluid being twice as strong as any other parameter, and the combined effect of cutting speed and feed rate being nearly as significant.

This article explores the connections between distance functions on graphs and metric spaces, allowing for possible distortions. By establishing an equivalence, we relate the conformal dimension of a graph to its induced distance and weighted graph distances. Specifically, for any $\delta$ in the range $0<\delta<1$, we show that a particular property holds for all graphs: there exists a $\delta$ such that the conformal dimension of a graph is greater than or equal to the conformal dimension of its $\delta$-approximated distance graph. This result further enables us to derive lower bounds on the conformal dimension of various metric spaces constructed from graphs, particularly showing that certain spaces have a conformal dimension of at least $1+\sqrt{2}$, which resolves an open question in the field.

We've conducted a thorough $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing analysis within the framework of next-to-leading order chiral perturbation theory, incorporating all relevant low-energy hadronic data. By driving the quark condensates to their physically natural values, our results allow for a non-arbitrary examination of the contribution made by next-to-leading order terms. Furthermore, our analysis re-evaluates the significance of $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing in hadronic physics.

The effectiveness of a signature forgery detection system heavily relies on the characteristics of the signature templates used to train it. These templates are created from authentic signatures, which possess unique properties such as distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability. A set of 1024 genuine signature images were collected from 226 signers at the University of Kent, along with their corresponding biographical details. Following the development of a trained discriminator model, the system was tested on 1920 forged signatures by 312 forgers to evaluate its performance. By examining the performance for different numbers of training templates per signer, the impact of varying template quality on the system's effectiveness was determined. Ultimately, the research found that the quality of the templates used to train the system has a significant effect on its overall performance.

This study focuses on how certain supersymmetry principles influence the behavior of low-energy effective couplings within string theory frameworks that include a Calabi-Yau compactification. Using a mathematical formalism based on superfields makes it feasible to examine these constraints in a model-independent manner, and our findings reveal that they significantly standardize the forms of effective coupling beta functions at low energy levels.

The influence of thermal effects on the behavior of correlation functions from at least the fourth order needs to be considered when analyzing quantum many-body systems that are coupled to thermal sources such as heat baths. This important factor is frequently overlooked in the study of quantum information and interactions within complex systems. We have developed a crucial set of mathematical relationships that establish the connection between the correlations observed in the target system and the correlations of the system and its surroundings. These relationships are based on the correlation functions of the coupled system and its environment. This finding provides a pathway to accurately assess the influence of thermal effects, which is particularly significant given the expanding field of quantum technologies that require thermal control and efficient cooling methods.

We introduce a new model for simulating galactic chemical evolution that accurately accounts for the complex relationships between various elements. By considering multiple factors such as star formation rates, initial mass function, and yield patterns for both massive and low-mass stars, our model effectively distinguishes between core and envelope contributions to the gas phase. It also takes into account the dynamic mass exchange between stars through binary interactions, which influences both nitrogen and oxygen abundance. As a result, our model replicates the observed correlations between [N/O] and [O/H] in the Milky Way and replicates the observed delayed [N/O] abundance relative to [O/H]. Furthermore, our model is applicable to other spiral and irregular galaxies and can be used to constrain various astrophysical processes.

Advancements in NLP research are greatly enhancing the lives of individuals in multilingual communities by providing accessible tools and technologies for communication, education, and information dissemination. The growing interest in NLP across diverse languages has been exemplified by the rapid expansion of key conferences such as Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL) 2021, which featured an extensive array of innovative research studies spanning multiple topics and languages. This digest aims to summarize the year's significant NLP research breakthroughs by highlighting the most notable publication outcomes in various research domains, including morphology, phonetics, and semantics, as well as applications in natural language understanding, generation, and processing.

In the analysis of intricate biological systems, where their underlying graphs represent essential characteristics, effective statistical methods are being developed to make informed decisions based on both graph topology and additional node attributes. The increasing accessibility of high-throughput data enables researchers to model and study these systems as large-scale networks. The resulting statistical analysis necessitates the consideration of both inherent network structure and additional node information. To address this requirement, a new model and corresponding inference algorithm are presented that blend both attributes and are scalable for big data applications. The proposed method is then applied to two real-world datasets to illustrate its practical utility.

We investigated the Left-Right Symmetric Model that features a bi-doublet field, assuming its conjugate as well, under the constraint of $Z$-boson mass as a fundamental physical constant. Given the known mass of the $Z$-boson, this model is confined to a specific boundary in a two-dimensional graph representing the coupling strengths of $W_R$ and $W$-bosons. To further delimit this parameter space, we analyzed the possibility of forming white dwarf stars, discovering a region within our constraint boundaries where this model's protons can form white dwarfs through gravitationally stable, non-degenerate matter composed of deuterium and other elements, with their mass ratio adhering to strict nuclear pairing rules.

Our Graph Privacy Advisor tool assesses and advises on the privacy of graphs such as road networks and social connections presented in image form. A user uploads these graphical images along with a caption to our website, where our advisory tool analyzes the image and the caption together to determine the level of privacy present. This level of privacy is then measured against established benchmarks in the field. Notably, our tool outperforms prior graph-based methods by 8% in the classification of privacy images and our advisory tool also accommodates captions, setting it apart from other relevant tools.

Two approaches have been proposed to quantify entropy generation in radiative fields from quantum effects, one based on the Kaellen-Lehavasseur model and the other on the Hott-Larsen-Papadodimas model, both originating from distinct holographic frameworks. In this study, a link between these two entropy formulas has been established, which holds universally across all spacetime settings, including both vacuum and non-vacuum states. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the difference in entropy values obtained from the two formulas is negligible compared to the horizon entropy, significantly small in both absolute and relative terms.

The ATLAS detector at the LHC has collected 0.3/nB 2015 and 0.025/nB 2018 Pb+Pb, 25/nB 2015 and 0.9/nB 2018 pp data. In central and inclusive events off- and online  jet  pT  corrections  for  400<|η|<1  were  analyzed.  In  central  events,  the  spectrum  shifted  towards  lower  pT  and  online  measurements  matched  offline  results.  In  inclusive  events,  the  spectrum  shifted  towards  higher  pT  and  online  measurements  matched  offline  results.  In  central  events,  the  shape  shifted  towards  wider  dispersion  and  online  measurements  matched  offline  results.  In  inclusive  events,  the  shape  shifted  towards  narrower  dispersion.  In  central  events  versus  inclusive  events,  the  spectrum  and  shape  exhibited  distinct  differences.

In the near future, advancements in computational methods are anticipated to
be influenced by the characteristics of upcoming low-precision hardware. To this
end, there is a pressing need to develop innovative approaches that effectively
exploit upcoming computing power. One potential approach is the use of
low-precision floating point arithmetic in high-level algorithms, and our paper
investigates the feasibility of this technique by examining several standard
mathematical functions. Our findings indicate that even with very limited precision,
values as low as 5 or 6 can be sufficient for numerous functions, and we also
determine the minimum precision required for each individual function.

The FOXSI instrument on board the International Space Station is the first to successfully observe the quiet Sun in hard X-rays. Achieving this is challenging due to the instrument's low sensitivity and the interference from cosmic background and the space station's own outgassing. To overcome these difficulties, FOXSI utilizes a reflective telescope and a localized multi-layer insulation system that serves as both heat reductor and X-ray detector. During its initial flight in 2014, FOXSI failed to detect the quiet Sun in hard X-rays, but its second flight in 2015 successfully did so, setting a new sensitivity record at that time. Building on this success, FOXSI's third flight in 2016 improved its sensitivity by emitting its own X-ray light, but its image of the quiet Sun remained unclear. FOXSI's designers are working on improving the instrument to better understand and replicate the conditions necessary to observe the quiet Sun in hard X-rays during its upcoming flights.

Identifying influential users within social networks is a valuable knowledge gap with far-reaching implications for social media engagement and marketing strategies. Previous research on this topic has been hindered by large amounts of unlabeled data and the need for accurate model scalability, making model training and predictions by sampling data even more challenging. To address these issues, we introduce a new framework that incorporates both train- and test-time data augmentation to break the traditional two-stage model prediction process. The impact of this innovation was found to be heavily dependent on graph size: extreme oversampling during training was beneficial, while aggressive sampling in testing added predictive value. Notably, the best results were achieved by reducing the number of labels required for training while using test-time augmentation to compensate for the limitations.

This paper explores the Euler-Arnold equations in the context of a specific model from quantum field theory, examining how these equations emerge from a control maximization problem that incorporates both velocity-dependent and velocity-independent constraints.

Recent advancements in sensor fusion for estimating object poses have been hindered by a fundamental issue: the inability to account for all possible sources of error. Current methods typically make two crucial assumptions - that errors are random and uncorrelated - but these assumptions are not always valid. In this research, we challenge these assumptions by developing a novel approach that acknowledges the existence of more comprehensive correlations in errors. By doing so, we've derived a new mathematical framework that enables the estimation of these correlated errors without relying on random assumptions. When tested on real-world data from multiple sources, our approach consistently outperformed existing methods, demonstrating the significance of including all error correlations for accurate sensor calibration and pose estimation.

Even if the universe has a single overall temperature, there can be significant variations in temperature across different scales, which can be significant during the early stages of the universe's formation. This work builds upon previous findings that demonstrated how these spatial temperature fluctuations enhance the process of dark matter annihilation and influence the minimum mass threshold for dark matter stars to form. This threshold is found to be substantially lower when the universe's temperature fluctuations are considered, which could lead to the rapid growth of dense regions of dark matter particles at an even earlier stage of the universe's evolution.

A search for identical bosons in events featuring high-mass, same-sign W boson pairs, where each W boson decomposes into a charged lepton and a neutrino, has been conducted using data collected by the CMS Collaboration at the LHC in 2017. A total of 47.1 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy were analyzed. Two distinct production methods, considered to be standard model predictions, were explored: (1) boson pairs arising from the decay of a Higgs boson, specifically a Higgs boson produced either directly or via a top quark, and (2) boson pairs resulting from the quartic coupling of gauge bosons. Additionally, a combination of these two contributions was considered. Observed occurrences were compared to expected standard model predictions. Specifically, the expected significance of the standard model predictions exceeded the observed data by 1.1 standard deviations for same-sign positive W boson pairs and by 0.2 standard deviations for same-sign negative W boson pairs. New interpretations of these results were also proposed.

This study introduces a versatile approach that transforms grayscale images into full-color versions by leveraging a library of pre-existing images. The proposed technique differs from existing methods by allowing the use of any single image as the reference for colorizing a given grayscale photo, rather than depending on multiple images for accurate results. Additionally, our approach has the capability to handle images of various subjects which were not previously accounted for in the library, by adapting the existing color information and applying it to the new image through iterative refinement. Extensive testing was conducted using the Google Brain framework to validate the performance of our method against other colorization techniques. The resulting outcomes show that our approach produces significantly better results that are both more realistic and effective, while also offering a more streamlined and efficient training process.

This study introduces a novel $P(q)$ model of cosmological parameters that accounts for spatial flatness and non-flat scenarios. By incorporating two free parameters - the Ricci scalar $R$ and curvature radius $q$ - this model can encompass a range of geometrical setups. When focusing on scenarios with a fixed value of $A_L=1$, this paper's models exhibit better agreement with Planck data and latex than their constant-horizon counterparts. Moreover, these models display improved compatibility with lunar and solar system data, although a slight penalty in likelihood results from the additional degree of freedom introduced by the model. In contrast, its performance in relation to BICEP2 and Keck array data lags behind the constant-horizon scenario. This paper's primary finding shows that the $P(q)$ model's likelihood surpasses that of $\Lambda$CDM when focusing on a fixed $A_L=1$ and $R=0$, but this advantage is lost when $A_L$ and $R$ are treated as free parameters. Nonetheless, the $P(q)$ model remains a viable candidate for parameter estimation in dark energy studies.

This study examines how collaborative coding projects maintain their files, 
revealing a noticeable disparity in the same files stored within multiple 
repository platforms. Our research yields practical insights for developing 
more effective techniques to identify shared files across various repository 
platforms and uncover the underlying maintenance practices underlying these 
coding collaborations.

Our current understanding of the binary system BD And suggests that it consists of two stars rotating together, although recent discoveries indicate the presence of a third star, known as star C. This star is believed to be a red dwarf that is not visibly distinct due to being overwhelmed by star A's radiation. Our study involved analyzing the light curve patterns of the system, using a Wilson-Devinney model to create detailed maps of the binary stars' characteristics. Our analysis also detected subtle irregularities in the light curve, which cannot be fully explained by the binary system's dynamics. These anomalies are more pronounced during certain phases, pointing to the influence of star C's eclipses. By factoring in the light contributed by star C, our models provide a more accurate representation of the binary system's dynamics.

This paper presents a case for approximating a maximal solution to the Yamabe flow, especially in situations where the initial data is not derived from a single manifold. We show that, in such instances, finite-time blowup occurs along with a corresponding compactification process. The study also confirms the existence of maximal solutions in scenarios where the initial data is derived from a single manifold, thus extending existing eigenfunction-based results. To facilitate these findings, a new approach is taken that involves approximating solutions using a series of manifolds whose metric evolves over time according to the Yamabe flow.

To effectively learn user preferences from incomplete and sparse data, a novel self-supervised method is proposed to improve recommendation systems. The method introduces two key components: the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement module and the Self-supervised Interactive dynamics model. The GAPE module identifies crucial aspect preferences by leveraging user-item interactions and a proposed Gating mechanism. The Self-supervised Interactive dynamics model then organically generates more item embeddings through interactive dynamics, which are subsequently fused with the initial embeddings using the GAPE module. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through experiments on three benchmark datasets, which show that it surpasses state-of-the-art self-supervised and supervised baselines in both training and testing modes.

We've developed an obstruction theory for symplectic sheaves in smooth projective varieties. The key  results can be represented by specific cohomology classes in the perfect obstruction theory for $\Symp^\sp$ as a funtor from the category of sheaves with a symplectic form to the category of hypercohomology spaces. The funtor $\Symp^\sp$ calculates the hypercohomology of a sheaf with a symplectic form, applying the de Rham complex. The obtained results provide an alternative to existing obstruction theory which involves the complex $\mathcal{E}^{\bullet,\bullet}$ and its hypercohomology space $H^{\bullet,\bullet}$.

This paper employs generating functions to derive asymptotics for sequences of integers that describe the number of partitions of a positive integer into distinct part multiplicities, constrained by a maximum limit for each part. Similar approaches have been applied in number theory to investigate the dual of the strong conjecture related to the Hardy--Ramanujan--Chandrasekhar conjecture concerning the largest prime divisors of terms in the nth power of the generating function for partitions of n.

We investigate weighted least squares methods for finite-dimensional linear approximation, focusing on exact sample data and potential corrupted data. By incorporating a suitable, positive-semidefinite weight matrix into the least squares objective, we can achieve both stability and optimality. We establish the expression for the optimal weight matrix and demonstrate its positive-semidefinite properties, enabling the use of its Cholesky decomposition. We further introduce an expectation-based approach for general non-uniformly distributed samples and provide specific weight matrices for important scenarios, including $l_2$-regression and kernel-based approximation. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees for a variant of the weighted least squares method when dealing with data corruption. We validate our approach with several experiments, including applications to kernel-based approximation and data fitting in the presence of outliers or anomalies.

The characteristics of the X(3872) was studied in a complex environment where two particles collide and form a compound object that subsequently breaks apart. This analysis took into account the internal structure of the X(3872) within a quantum field theory framework, focusing on its reaction rates and initial configurations in the hadronic phase. Our results indicate that the X(3872)'s decay constants are substantially lower when its internal structure is not considered. Consequently, the reaction rates and initial configurations are significantly amplified when the X(3872)'s internal structure is accounted for. Notably, the most probable initial configuration occurs when the two particles from the collision are rapidly moving in the same direction and the compound object is predominantly transversely oriented.

A detailed examination of the magnetic properties of silicon phosphorus was conducted using a combination of theoretical and numerical methods. The study employed a dynamic mean-field theory, taking into account both the spin-orbit interaction and electron-electron interactions in a two-band model. It was discovered that these interactions produce a significant local magnetic moment, similar to transition metal compounds, yet the valence states are distinct. The theoretical findings accurately matched experimental data for the susceptibility and hyperfine coupling constant, particularly in relation to the number of magnetic electrons per phosphorus atom.

The paper develops a comprehensive framework for the generalized standard model of the finite classical Coxeter group Bn. It derives key properties and relations for each Bn orbit within the affine Bruhat order, particularly concerning their partitioning according to Coxeter length and a generalized Galois set. The properties and interactions between these sets, along with the Galois set itself, are thoroughly examined. The proof of an induction hypothesis on these properties is also outlined.

We analyzed the conservation of U(1) current in several scalar field theories, taking into account both explicit and hidden symmetry breaking terms. In a framework where the U(1) symmetry is strictly observed, we derived the interaction of the U(1) current with a massless fermion in these theories. Our research specifically examined the cases of a Wess-Zumino model, a nonlinear sigma model and a superfield model, all with the U(1) symmetry preserved. Our results show that the U(1) current remains strictly conserved in these theories, unless a fermion is included, in which case the conservation depends on the specific model.

When robots learn from experienced humans, they must account for various factors, such as the qualities of both the humans and the objects being worked on. Despite the effectiveness of statistical learning methods in handling these variables, they require complete data sets, which can be difficult to obtain in practical settings due to the high costs involved. As an alternative, we present a sophisticated modeling approach that utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian framework to tackle this challenge. This method enables us to leverage domain-specific knowledge about the likely characteristics of human instructors and the objects being worked on. By doing so, we can improve the performance of the learning process using only partial data and without the need for direct supervision. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a series of simulations focused on a pick-and-place task within a real-world setting.

The paper explores various topological properties on the space $\widetilde{X}_H$ and establishes a Whitney retraction from $X$ to $\widetilde{X}_H$ when $X$ possesses the Whitney property. It is demonstrated that the whisker topology and the lasso topology are equivalent and coincide with the compactly symmetric topology on $\widetilde{X}_H$. Furthermore, the paper shows that the continuous Whitney retraction from $X$ to $\widetilde{X}_H$ is also a whisker-continuous and a lasso-continuous retraction. The paper also establishes that the whisker topology and the lasso topology are first-countable and locally compact on $\widetilde{X}_H$.

This paper presents a Deep Reinforcement Learning approach that integrates motion planning and control. The method, consisting of a single-stage solution that combines planning and control, is particularly well-suited for complex tasks. Unlike conventional methods that separate these stages, our solution has demonstrated success in tasks such as simulating a driver's behavior and controlling a quadrotor.

Our research explores how black holes grow through dynamic interactions with surrounding gas and stars using high-resolution simulations. We examine the impact of a small radiative feedback force on the mass of a central black hole over the course of a typical star-forming period. With each simulation step, a black hole efficiently gobbles up gas from an accretion disk, acquiring a substantial mass - approximately one to two times the mass of the sun - before being overwhelmed by a burst of nearby gas. We observe that feedback from nearby stars fails to significantly affect black hole growth, whereas moderate levels of star cluster feedback can prevent a black hole from growing too large. In the long term, a black hole can be actively feeding, but only if it is located at the center of a large galaxy.

Deep neural networks have become a preferred method for addressing complex classification tasks. However, their reliability and accuracy can be compromised in the presence of noisy labels or unreliable training data. This paper utilizes Bayesian modelling to develop an accurate and reliable deep learning system capable of learning label distributions, predicting confidence levels, and handling uncertain situations effectively. By incorporating a Bayesian neural network with a robust prior, we have developed a novel approach that outperforms the current state-of-the-art method on synthetic data and shows comparable results on real-world data sets while showcasing its ability to effectively handle uncertainty through a series of rigorous experiments.

The widespread use of preprints in scientific research has led to a rise in questions about their effect on publication methods in biology. A recent cross-sectional study involved data from arXiv and bioRxiv to compare preprint and published versions of research articles in theoretical biology. Key differences and disparities between these versions were examined for their scientific content. The majority of papers in this study showed minimal to no variations in their content, whereas a small percentage of papers exhibited significant differences. Those papers with notable discrepancies often received higher citation counts and had a longer gap between their preprint and published dates. The results suggest that some preprints may experience prolonged review processes, while others are rapidly accepted and published. A possible solution to these issues is for journals to adopt more streamlined submission and review processes for papers with established impact.

One of the primary goals in biotechnology and medicine is to validate that laboratory equipment functions correctly. This is crucial because malfunctioning equipment can lead to inaccurate test results, which may have severe consequences. To ensure the reliability of laboratory instruments, they must undergo regular calibration checks. Currently, these calibration processes are labor-intensive, as they involve manually documenting the results of each test, which is time-consuming and error-prone. To tackle this issue, we developed an automated data management system that significantly reduces human error. By integrating our system with the existing laboratory information management systems (LIMS), we enable the efficient flow of data from the measurement software to the LIMS, thus eliminating the need for manual intervention. This innovative approach not only saves time but also prevents human mistakes, while providing a clear audit trail in case of any discrepancies.

Machine learning (ML) techniques are rapidly gaining traction in the field of materials science due to their remarkable ability to quickly generate vast amounts of data with high accuracy. Building on this momentum, our research explores the potential of ML algorithms in predicting the structural and mechanical properties of multi-element alloys through a thermally induced phase transformation. By leveraging simulations of thermal treatments, we can determine the phase composition and mechanical properties associated with specific temperature and composition variables. The collected datasets are then employed to train and evaluate the performance of various ML models. Notably, our results indicate that the phase compositions and mechanical properties predicted by the ML models exhibit a strong match with experimental data obtained through x-ray diffraction and nanoindentation experiments. The success of these predictions underscores the potential of ML algorithms as a powerful tool for enhancing materials design, particularly in identifying optimal compositions and phase combinations that are difficult to locate using traditional methods.

To investigate the interactions of the intermediate $D^*D$ and $D^*\tau$ states in the $T_{cc}^{++}$ decay within the framework of QED and QCD, we have analyzed the contributions of these interactions, which are comparable, although both can lead to a significant reduction in the branching ratio of the $T_{cc}^{++}$ three-body decay to $D^*D\tau$. Our analysis shows that these interactions primarily affect the kinematics of the final state particles. A more detailed examination of the contributions of these interactions to specific kinematic endstates is necessary to fully understand their effects.

Recent advancements in machine learning have seen increased focus on subspace learning, a challenge also present in graph representation learning where extracting key subgraphs from complex graphs becomes essential. To tackle this issue, a new approach is introduced that combines graph neural networks to develop capable subspace learners. By integrating a graph encoder and a subspace learner into a unified framework, the method produces high-quality subgraphs that exceed the performance of existing benchmarks. Furthermore, the algorithm is versatile and accommodates various graph encoder and subspace learner modules, demonstrating its applicability in multiple graph representation learning tasks.

In this study, we delve into the completeness problem of Sidon sets within the finite affine plane, a challenge initially posed as a collective effort by the Hungarian Mathematical Association. Our research expands on past findings from Schneider and Forrill-Batchelder by redefining Sidon sets in the affine plane as set $A \subset \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}^2$ that has the property of $0$ and $1$ not being in the same equivalence class within $\left(\mathbb{Z}_m^2,\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\right)$. Additionally, by translating this structure into the hyperbolic plane and ellipsoidal plane, we demonstrate that solutions to the Sidon set problem can be mapped one-to-one onto solutions in these other geometric configurations. As a result, the Sidon set problem is now shown to be an instance of an even more complex and extensively researched issue - the completeness problem of hyperbolic triangles and ellipses - a problem initially explored by Dür in 1934 and later by Dörkson in 2018.

Current methods for sampling binary matrices are either inefficient or very costly. Additionally, commonly used uniform distribution sampling leads to a considerable amount of irrelevant data. To address this issue, this study proposes sampling binary matrices using a non-uniform probability distribution, specifically the hypergeometric distribution, based on the underlying structure of these matrices. The number of non-zero elements in these matrices can be seen as a random variable that follows a Poisson distribution. By sampling from this distribution, more focused and relevant data can be obtained, especially when the distribution's parameters are well-informed. The performance of this sampling method is compared to that of efficient but uniform sampling methods, and the results show a substantial decrease in time required to obtain similar levels of accuracy.

A novel approach to parton distribution function (PDF) fitting utilizes differential equation-based evolution of PDFs at various scales, thereby incorporating the DGLAP equations. This method is a part of a broader class of operator product expansion solutions to PDFs, which also encompasses other evolution schemes such as the DGLAP and EREB schemes. Unlike traditional PDF fitting methods that require numerous steps to account for the DGLAP equations, this approach simplifies the fitting process by merging the evolution and fitting stages into a single, complex operation. Nevertheless, it was discovered that direct application of the DGLAP equations to experimental data is impractical due to data being presented at fixed momentum transfers and not being compatible across different scales. To overcome these obstacles, this method employs a truncated kernel to apply the DGLAP evolution to mock PDFs, and also includes a framework for propagating uncertainties. Furthermore, the feasibility of using this approach to fit experimental data at different momentum transfers using a quadratic fit is explored.

This paper introduces a revamped version of the ELKI data mining framework, 
upgrading it with improved scalability and efficiency via process distribution 
within a shared-memory environment. The updated implementation employs parallel 
data structures and algorithms to balance computation and overlap step loading, 
thereby achieving a balanced dissemination of work among all available processor 
cores. The enhanced framework also integrates a dynamic load balancer to dynamically 
adjust the partitioning of tasks based on the real-time computation load of each 
process. The objective of these modifications is to substantially boost the 
performance of large-scale data mining operations by disseminating the workload 
across multiple processor cores and achieving a more even distribution of tasks.

We present a novel method to generate a highly controllable, discrete-frequency microcomb spectrum, utilizing the nonlinearity in a microresonator. By aligning the pump laser's sidebands at specific, evenly spaced intervals, we create a unique microcomb pattern. This specialized spacing can be achieved by adjusting the pump laser's frequency or the microresonator's frequency, offering high precision due to the microresonator's stable frequency output. This technique enhances our ability to produce a desired, complex microcomb spectrum and may find applications in high-precision spectroscopy and communication systems.

We've established that for any non-trivial element $\alpha$ in the Heisenberg group, a random subgroup generated by a random walk of finite memory has two distinct and irreducible properties: it is both strongly mixing and faithful. Additionally, we derived a more general criterion for characteristic subgroups with these same properties in any nilpotent group of finite step and a solvable group of a specific type with a long prime characteristic.

This paper explores the inner workings of quasi neural networks, a type of neural network approximation that yields exact predictions at specific input/output pairs. By applying a tangent kernel representation, we demonstrate that quasi neural networks can be transformed into a regular neural network, whose properties are equivalent to a standard gradient-based empirical risk minimization. Importantly, our findings reveal that the learning process of this quasi neural network converges to the standard neural network, provided the decay rate of a particular eigenvalue is greater than or equal to a certain threshold. Conversely, if this eigenvalue declines at a slower rate, the learning process differs substantially from its standard counterpart. To illustrate these discrepancies, we present simulation examples.

A study investigates a holographic theory with boundary, assuming its monogamy of mutual information among bulk regions as well as their semi-holographic property. Derived in this research are specific constraints on boundary entropies. It's demonstrated that satisfying these constraints enables the reconstruction of bulk information from boundary data, without the need for additional information from the bulk. Furthermore, the findings imply that the strong bulk singularity at the center of Schwarzschild black holes is uniquely defined by the boundary entropy of a surrounding cylinder. Lastly, the results suggest that the boundary entropy of a disk surrounding a strong bulk singularity can be expressed solely in terms of the boundary entropy of a surrounding cylinder.

Two-dimensional lattice models, including the free-fermion model, the Yang-Baxter model, and the star-triangle model, are examined to establish a connection between their local state probabilities and a branching rule. This connection enables the derivation of a probability expression solely based on the model's solvability, independent of any underlying fermionic representation. For applicable models, this expression can be used to calculate the partition function and central charge of associated topological orders. Additionally, the study of critical points on the torus using this approach reveals how to compute conformal field theory parameters, including the conformal dimension and stress tensor, through an analytical solution, as validated by the free-fermion model case.

This research investigates the effectiveness of combining separate stabilization methods with interior point methods for solving convex optimization problems. We draw on existing theories to demonstrate that the combination of two stabilizers yields a single, unified stabilizer. Furthermore, we derive a condition under which the combined interior point method is equivalent to an interior point method enhanced by the combined stabilizer. Through numerical experiments, we validate the interior point method when applied to problems involving absolute values and box constraints.

Traditional nonlinear coaddition algorithms such as median and weighted mean can't maintain a consistent point spread function (PSF) because they're inherently designed to prioritize accuracy of flux measurements. We developed two new algorithms that utilize clipping to filter outliers while preserving the PSF: one works by calculating the mean of clipped fluxes and the other applies a clipping radius to the fluxes before coadding them. These methods are shown to be equivalent and consistently produce coadds with a smooth, constant PSF for point sources. We also found that the choice of clipping limits has a minimal impact on the final coadds. These algorithms are suitable for a variety of imaging data and are particularly useful for producing shallow, wide-field surveys like the VHS.

We establish that chordal SLE($\\gamma$) evolves into imaginary surfaces within the Riemann sphere minus three distinct points, a construction first presented by Saary by combining conformal mappings with Johansson's independent work. Furthermore, a natural parametrization by time allows us to prove that this evolution remains stationary under a group of conformal inversions centered at these points. Building on this insight, we demonstrate that SLE($2$) also remains invariant under the duality involution $(z \mapsto 1/z)$ found in Jimenez's work and found another independent proof using a different approach.

This paper aims to provide an alternative proof for the Navier-Stokes equations' $L^p$ bound, specifically focused on the $L^\infty$ norm, which can be found in the work of Kato and Masuda. Our approach builds upon the fundamental ideas of the Navier-Stokes equations' energy estimate and Maxwell's equation, resulting in a bound of the form $\|u\|_{L^\infty(0,T; L^\infty)} \leq C e^{Ct} (\|u(0)\|_{L^\infty} + t^{1/2} \|u\|_{L^p(0,T; L^p)}).$

This paper proposes a complex visual question answering protocol that leverages deep learning, allowing for both accurate answer verification and visual proof without requiring clients to share their computation details with the server. We designed the CVQC protocol to address the limitations of existing Q&A protocols that rely on quantum computing, which often demand significant computational resources from clients and may compromise on verification accuracy due to oversimplified protocol structures. In contrast, our CVQC protocol is constructed using a series of interactive queries, where the server generates prompters and the client computes answers while keeping their computation details private. We then develop a verification algorithm using a series of interactive queries, enabling the server to confirm the accuracy of the answers without needing access to the client's computation details. Furthermore, our CVQC protocol features multiple advantages over the existing AQC-QQC protocol: 1) faster verification speeds; 2) more accurate verification results; 3) reduced dependence on computational resources; and 4) improved resistance to tampering and logical errors. We validate the performance of our CVQC protocol through both theoretical analysis and practical testing, demonstrating its superior capabilities over the existing solution.

The versatility of deep generative models makes them suitable for a variety of discrete and continuous data synthesis tasks. In the context of image analysis, learning-based approaches can be used to generate cell shapes, aiding in segmentation and tracking processes, while also enriching our understanding of cellular morphology and its role in development and disease. A new class of shape synthesis techniques based on GPCs offers improved control over generated shapes compared to previously existing methods. However, these models have not been previously applied to the synthesis of 3D cell-like point clouds, which is a challenging task due to the complexity of cellular morphology. To address this gap, we present a method that uses Gaussian Processes to regulate the symmetry of cell-like shapes generated with Proximity-based Conditional GPCs, effectively creating controlled 3D cell synthesis. Our approach enables the generation of cell-like shapes with desired symmetry properties, presenting novel results in the field of cell biology that can be utilized for segmentation and tracking purposes in simulations of cell migration and division.

Reinforcement learning experiments were conducted to examine how feature persistence affects geometric tasks. Building upon earlier research that found persistent features improve performance, we explored the opposite - tasks where features do not persist. A custom environment was created with a flat terrain, character movement, and goal locations at varying distances. Agents were instructed to navigate to these goals as quickly as possible. To evaluate the impact of feature persistence, the time taken by agents to complete tasks was compared in both environments. The results indicated that agents perform better in environments where features persist. This outcome contradicts the initial hypothesis that non-persistent features could lead to improved performance.

To capture the dynamics of three-dimensional dipolar systems, we developed a numerical method, ECMC, based on the Newtonian variant of that algorithm.
