This approach successfully resolves the angle variables issue in these models, which had previously prevented the use of molecular dynamics simulations. Our method also addresses the challenge of dynamical arrest, a common issue in dipolar systems. We tested our Newtonian ECMC variant by simulating a collection of dipolar soft-sphere particles and examining its ability to maintain the system's equilibrium. Our results show that the Newtonian ECMC variant is capable of accurately modeling the dynamics of these systems across various polarities and densities, a performance that surpasses a modified Langevin dynamics method.

Data augmentation plays a significant role in improving deep neural network-based sound event detection, regardless of whether it enhances training or testing processes. This study delves into various methods of data augmentation for sound classification, including audio signal transformations, network-generated extensions, and labeling techniques. The benefits of incorporating data augmentation into a system are thoroughly analyzed through experimental results obtained from the DCASE 2019 challenge tasks, including independent validation and comparison with a baseline model. To optimize the effectiveness of data augmentation, a method for selecting the most useful transformations from a given set of options is proposed. The findings of this study are meant to guide other researchers in the field in choosing data augmentation techniques most suitable for their sound classification tasks.

The superposition property, allowing multiple messages to be transmitted in a single channel, has significant implications for various applications such as federated learning and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). This property's potential in nomalizations, a key component of deep learning, suggests a promising direction for this research area. Motivated by the superposition property's potential, the present study proposes a new framework called SOT. SOT takes advantage of the superposition property in nomalizations by superposing multiple gradient messages in a single update step. SOT's implementation is straightforward and only requires minor adjustments to existing neural networks. Experimental results indicate that SOT achieves notable performance improvements while reducing communication efficiency. Specifically, SOT outperforms baseline models by up to 10% in terms of top-1 accuracy and reduces communication costs by a factor of 10 to 20.

This research introduces a novel technique to extract meaningful information from complex data sets, which involves applying a spectral analysis using the Spectrogram Level Set Transform (SLST). The Spectrogram Level Set Transform is an extension of the Level Set method, combining spectrogram analysis with level sets to identify relevant structures within the spectrogram's natural scale. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective in multiple scenarios, including both discrete and continuous signal processing, and is compared to established techniques such as the Persistent Homology algorithm. Results show that the Spectrogram Level Set Transform outperforms Persistent Homology in several aspects, including accuracy, computational efficiency, and robustness to noise, noise resilience, and ability to generalise to new data. Additionally, the paper explores the application of SLST to classification tasks in machine learning, employing a supervised approach to evaluate its performance.

We present a novel method to identify and analyze the synchronized states of a given complex dynamical system. By employing a cluster-based approach, we determine the number of synchronized clusters and their respective frequencies, as well as the within-cluster phase relationships among system variables. This method is applicable even in situations where direct observation of the system's state is challenging or impossible, and it requires only access to a limited set of measured output variables. We evaluate the efficacy of our proposed method using a widely used chaotic oscillator network for which we also introduce a new approach to accurately calculate the exact number of synchronized clusters.

We have developed a novel, user-friendly module within Blender called "Physics for Blender" to simulate complex physical systems. This module utilizes the DyRE engine, enabling accurate simulations of elastic collisions, explicit collision mapping, and rigid-body dynamics, among other features. Unlike existing solutions, this module seamlessly integrates with Blender's geometry, allowing users to define physical properties at the vertex, edge, and face levels. As a result, users can easily set up simulations involving thousands of moving particles, leveraging optimized data structures and multi-threaded processing. Furthermore, users can customize simulations using a vast array of effects, such as springs, dampers, and explicit controls, and visualize the results using a range of rendering techniques, including particle systems and smooth surface rendering.

The performance of an information engine called a "QARNG" is examined when its system is being continuously observed. Differing from earlier studies where the system was instantaneously measured, this study explores the effect of a real-time measurement process. Building on standard quantum optics principles, it's shown that the system's ability to extract work from an energy source is significantly impacted by the measurement process, and in fact, it's only possible to extract a limited amount of energy when the system is continuously measured. This finding is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics.

Jamming in a two-dimensional space of freely falling disks is examined with varying disk weights and a fixed, horizontally oriented, confined channel. When lighter and heavier disks are introduced into the system, they do not reach the same jammed state despite having different weights. Introducing a large number of extremely heavy disks allows these disks to occupy the bottom layer of the system, revealing a distinct jamming threshold based solely on the fraction of heavy disks. These results indicate that the conventional definition of jamming is not applicable in situations involving disks of significantly varying weights. A modified definition of jamming is proposed to accommodate such scenarios.

Using satellite measurements and machine learning techniques, researchers identified two distinct flavors in each El Ni$\tilde{\text{n}}$a (warm event) and La Ni$\tilde{\text{n}}$a (cool event), characterized by different precipitation patterns in the eastern Pacific. These flavors were found to significantly impact downpours in the region, with implications for global climate variability and extreme weather events, such as heavy precipitation and floods in the Amazon and East African savannas, respectively, associated with a particular flavor of La Ni$\tilde{\text{n}}$a. Researchers used neural networks to analyze satellite data from 20 years (2007-2019), identifying two distinct flavors in each El Ni$\tilde{\text{n}}$a and La Ni$\tilde{\text{n}}$a events, which were then linked to corresponding Amazon and African precipitation patterns. These findings were validated through multiple approaches, including a comprehensive statistical analysis, and further research is needed to understand the physical mechanisms driving these distinct flavors and their regional and global impacts.

We've developed a set of dynamical models for the growth of supermassive black holes, focusing on the intermediate stage before they reach their full potential. Our goal is to understand the mass distribution of black holes at this stage, especially how it relates to their spinal velocity. By utilizing a set of analytical and numerical models, we've explored how a black hole's mass and velocity evolve over time, especially its final mass and spin. Our results show a significant difference in the predicted mass and spin distributions between two scenarios: one where small, dense objects form black holes and another where lighter material does the same. Our predictions match observed data for the mass and spin relationship in more massive black holes. We've also found that less massive black holes tend to have lower spins, which could help explain a previously observed trend.

On flat band-driven correlations in novel geometric patterns, such as kagome and hyperkagome lattices, with multiple orbital configurations, where various effects like superconductivity, Mott transition, and ferromagnetism can be observed. A specific type of geometric pattern, known as the $\bar{4}3m$ lattice, which contains both chiral and non-chiral properties, is particularly noteworthy. Flat band-induced correlations in this type of lattice structure can be found when it is emulated using a square lattice with specific types of orbital configurations, where two orbital configurations, known as $ab$ and $c$, exhibit distinct properties. Flat band-induced correlations in this type of geometric pattern, which possesses $\bar{4}3m$ symmetry, can give rise to unique properties such as superconductivity, where the superconducting order parameter is tied to a specific wave vector, known as $\Gamma$.

By analyzing data from the Genome-Wide Association study of 29,000 individuals, our research identified nearly 15,000 genotype associations. We examined the proteins influenced by these variants and found that their impact generally extends beyond the protein itself, affecting neighboring molecules. Focusing on phenotype-related SNPs, we revealed that the influence of a protein sequence varies widely across different traits, but on average, the top 10% of affected proteins account for these associations. Moreover, we observed that proteins involved in these variants tend to have high mutation rates and are located in areas of the cell where interactions between different molecules occur.

A comprehensive study into the automorphism groups of 2-designs with a prime power number of points is presented in this paper. It has been proven that if sigma acts fixed-point freely on a prime power $q$ and $G$ is a $Gq$-invariant 2-design with no invariants except the identity, then $G$ can be classified into one of eight distinct non-trivial groups. It has further been established that a 2-design with a prime power number of points and no non-trivial invariants, except the identity, must have an automorphism group that is also a 2-design.

A unified mathematical framework is established to study the interplay between Coulomb correlation effects and the confinement of electrons in tiny nanostructures. By employing the Wigner-Renyi informational entropy, a classification of the Coulomb correlation is introduced based on the order of the entropy exponent (r=1,2,...). The framework is then applied to two types of confined electronic systems: a quantum dot with a linear confining potential and a carbon nanotube with a harmonic potential. The numerical results demonstrate that higher orders of the Coulomb correlation exponent are necessary to accurately calculate the energetic and positional uncertainties within these systems. Notably, the study finds that the Coulomb correlation effects are more pronounced in carbon nanotubes due to their smaller average inradius.

The precise measurement of binary star systems' velocity dispersion is crucial for understanding their formation and evolution. Current methods that measure 1D velocity dispersion are only applicable to a small number of stars and require at least 5 observable orbits. We have developed a new approach that uses line velocity information to accurately measure 1D velocity dispersion even with just 2 observable orbits. This method works by accounting for the effects of elliptical shape and stellar mass on line velocities. We tested our method with simulated data and real data from 9 wide binary star systems. The results show that line velocity information improves the accuracy of 1D velocity dispersion measurements and that including all line velocities gives more precise results than just using the mean line velocity. We compared our results with the standard method of using period and eccentricity to measure 1D velocity dispersion and found that for most systems, our new approach provides more precise results. However, the standard method is more accurate when the line velocity information is poor. We applied our new approach to 46 binary star systems and found that their 1D velocity dispersion is generally lower than expected for systems formed in the protoplanetary disk.

We introduce a method for deriving cut-elimination in multiplicative linear logic through a novel sequent calculus. This calculus is adapted from the $\lambda$-calculus by incorporating the notion of ideal representations to mirror the properties of proof structures in multiplicative linear logic. Ideal representations serve as a direct translation of the logical content embedded within these proof structures, allowing for the direct translation of cut-inference into the composition of ideal representations. By applying this approach, we can leverage the fundamental properties of ideal representations to establish a method for cut-elimination in this adapted calculus, thereby obtaining cut-elimination for the original multiplicative linear logic through a straightforward restriction on derivability.

This study examines the capability of deep learning models in predicting the synchronization status of time series pairs, similar to a previous approach that used a recurrent neural network to classify time series relationships. Our research extends the scope by including more markets and assets. A classification task is undertaken to identify whether time series pairs are in sync or out of sync based on their time lag and correlation. The results indicate that deep learning models can effectively predict synchronization states with a high level of accuracy for certain time lag values. Notably, our classification task achieved a high overall accuracy of 83.5% and revealed that the predictiveness of time lag values varies significantly across assets and assets pairs.

The goal is to manipulate a chemical reaction's quantum states across its potential energy surface by leveraging vibrations that can be controlled quantally. To achieve this, we couple a two-dimensional quantum system to its classical nuclear degrees of freedom. The nuclear vibrations are represented by two separate modes, which are connected to the reactive quantum state via two control fields. The system is initially in a non-reactive quantum state, and we apply multi-dimensional quantum control to drive it to a reactive state, and use the two control fields to adjust its trajectory across the potential energy surface. Our analysis shows that the nuclear vibrations can be controlled so that they guide the reactive quantum state across the reaction barrier. The key insight is that the two control fields can synchronize the two nuclear modes, either making them oscillate in sync or out of sync, which enables their use in fine-tuning the reactive quantum state's trajectory.

In the realm of click-through prediction for online advertising, the issues of bias and lack of transparency in models have received significant attention. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel benchmark called AdID, which comprises a large dataset of ad identifiers accompanied by relevant contextual information. This benchmark enables researchers to develop and evaluate their own click-through prediction models that incorporate the details of individual ads, thereby potentially mitigating bias and enhancing transparency. Furthermore, we highlight the importance of visual ID characteristics in predicting clicks and provide a straightforward implementation of a new model called Neo-CP3, which integrates ad identities into the framework of contextual parameterization, along with two additional methods of incorporating ID characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of Neo-CP3 over existing models in achieving both higher accuracy and improved transparency in click-through prediction.

The concept of fairness in concurrent systems has received considerable attention, 
yet its implementation remains complicated when business process models incorporate 
unbounded data and a measure of time. This study investigates the fair execution of 
business processes that involve an unlimited number of data objects and capacity-bounded 
queues. It defines a set of basic, compositionally feasible, and practically applicable 
fairness conditions based on process milestones. These conditions incorporate both 
data and time considerations. The study demonstrates that these conditions can be 
satisfied through a combination of two infinite processes and a finite number of 
processes with timing restrictions. The approach relies on previously established results 
regarding the concurrent execution of data operations and involves constructing a timing 
process from a given flow process using an algorithm that involves a linear number of 
operations. This construction is based on a graph representation and takes into account 
data and time constraints.

This study employs a statistical method that draws from physics to model the propagation of light pollution from wildfires, which is an area of limited research. By incorporating known principles such as the scattering theory, the model can simulate the counterintuitive behavior of light scattering in the atmosphere, which is essential for accurately characterizing the source of the pollution. The model is then applied to real-world data from a wildfire in California, which demonstrates its capability to provide quantitative results that align with observational data.

Private data publication maintains privacy by using data substitution or generalization. However, these methods are not suitable for conditional data and can be difficult to achieve a precise balance between privacy and utility. Our solution to this problem involves introducing a novel privacy model that protects private data by generalizing locations in a graph-based setting. This model also accounts for the conditional relationships between data points. To protect this model, we develop a quantitative framework that utilizes reconfiguration to ensure privacy and maximize utility. Our methods are tested on real-world datasets, showing that this approach yields better results compared to existing methods.

This study integrated a Bayesian model selection framework with a Bayesian network approach to examine inter-site synchronization in brain networks. We aimed to address two primary questions: Firstly, how do inter-site phenomena influence the accuracy of identifying individual and group-level distinctions in brain networks? Secondly, what inter-site connectivity patterns underpin these differences? To answer these queries, we developed a Bayesian framework that accounts for variability between sites and compared it with a literature-standard meta-analysis technique using fixed effects statistics. Our results revealed that inter-site effects enhance the detection of significant differences, and a site-specific network structure was identified as the source of these discrepancies. Furthermore, we found that combining data from all sites failed to uncover the distinct network topologies underlying each group, highlighting the importance of inter-site phenomena in understanding brain function and connectivity.

We introduce a novel concentration of measure inequality inspired by the heat flow. The time-evolving heat distribution on the torus, $f_t(x)$, where $f_0(x)$ is an arbitrary function, serves as the basis for our concentration inequality. Specifically, our inequality asserts that for all $t \geq 0$, the total variance of $f_t(x)$ is bounded by a function of both the temperature (denoted $\beta$) and time. This inequality is a direct consequence of a generalized log-Sobolev inequality. Our approach to establishing this inequality involves a two-step process: first, we derive a generalized log-Sobolev inequality for the heat kernel on the torus; second, we utilize a device introduced by Gross to obtain our desired concentration inequality.

Recent advancements in large language models have achieved remarkable success in processing monolingual data, yet their performance lags in handling code-mixed text effectively, a common phenomenon observed in online text feedback data and language models trained on the internet. This paper investigates how to adapt pre-trained models to process code-mixed data by incorporating four techniques: utilizing two different input forms, applying multi-task learning, and implementing positional and cross-positional encoding methods. The proposed strategies are evaluated in two scenarios - when the language model is trained on code-mixed data and when it is not. The results indicate that a combination of using two different input forms and multi-task learning yields the most significant improvement when the model is not trained on code-mixed data, while a specific combination of methods provides the best outcome when the model is trained on such data.

H$_3$S, a material exhibiting high tunability of its superconducting properties, provides an ideal setting to explore isotope effect beyond conventional materials like mercury, where both nuclear and electron masses impact the isotope effect coefficient ($\beta$). Utilizing first-principles calculations and Eliashberg equations, we investigated how the nuclear and electron masses contribute to $\beta$ under varying pressures. As the electron mass effect diminishes with increasing pressure, eventually becoming negligible above 140 GPa, the nuclear mass effect starts to dominate, aligning $T_c$ variations and predicting a nuclear mass driven $T_c$ dome. Our findings also suggest that the structural transformation from a microporous to a layered structure has a significant effect on the electron density of states and $T_c$.

In evolutionary biology, the average effect of a gene substitution is often compared to the change in a linear trait measure, but such a comparison typically relies on the linearity of the relationship between the genetic effect and the measured trait change, which may not always hold true. We provide a more general mathematical proof that the average effect of a gene substitution is equal to the fourth derivative of the population's or an individual's phenotype distribution, evaluated at the optimal genotype, multiplied by the variance of the underlying trait values. This proof assumes no linear relationship between the genetic effects and trait measures. We apply this theorem to continuous and discrete fitness functions, yielding novel insights into the dynamics of these models.

This research focuses on the control of two-legged robots, exploring how feedback from their environment and internal dynamics can be utilized to adapt their gait patterns. A nonlinear controller, reminiscent of a biological feedback loop, is employed to adjust walking speeds while maintaining balance. Through a stability analysis using the Lyapunov stability concept, it is demonstrated that this feedback-based control approach results in a stable and predictable gait cycle, even in the presence of external disturbances and unknown terrain inclinations. Successful outcomes from full-state feedback control simulations are documented, and further research is indicated for environments where some controller inputs are inaccessible to the robot.

We've developed a novel learning approach to creating camera pose descriptors that
outperform existing methods in challenging scenarios and serve as an optimal
baseline for future research in camera relocalization. By combining descriptors
with a straightforward correspondence matching system, we've created a robust
camera pose estimator that surpasses state-of-the-art performance in six out of
seven benchmark datasets, even when compared to methods using only trained
features. Our method's efficiency and effectiveness are further demonstrated by
its performance in demanding scenarios, such as those with low image resolution,
few correspondences, or repeated patterns, as well as its ability to estimate camera
poses in 3D without requiring any prior information.

In the personalization domain of federated learning, a challenge arises when personalizing models to individual clients while maintaining collaboration. Since each client has limited labeled data, this often leads to overfitting when updating models with their local data. To address this issue, we have developed a novel technique combining semi-supervised learning and personalized learning with few-shot adaptation. Our approach, called Distillation-Based Personalized Semi-Supervised Learning (DipSSL), first uses a broad data set to train a general semi-supervised model by integrating data and knowledge from multiple sources. It then distills this knowledge into a new, personalized model tailored to each client using their limited labeled data. To refine this model, DipSSL leverages the client's unlabeled data and their existing model through a mixture of Moor's attack and defense strategy. Our experimental results show that DipSSL significantly improves performance compared to both conventional and state-of-the-art approaches.

The disruption of a neutron star by another star results in an accretion-ejection column that forms in the disk. Early simulations indicate that magnetic fields are concentrated at the inner parts of the disk, specifically near the site of the disrupted neutron star. Initially, the magnetic energy within the inner parts of the disk surpasses the kinetic energy, but as the system evolves, the magnetic field progressively loses strength throughout the disk, primarily driven by dissipation in turbulent processes. In the aftermath of the disruption, the disk displays enhanced magnetic field turbulence, which in turn accelerates angular momentum transfer and viscous dissipation. Contrary to expectations, simulations reveal that the magnetic field's influence diminishes over time, particularly in the inner sections of the disk where it initially exerts a considerable impact.

For a compact Riemann surface, X, we examine the moduli space of sheaves, M, and identify its first Mumford-Morita-Miller class as the topological invariant that matches the determinant line bundle's first Chern class, specifically det(R^1p_*O_X), where p is the projection map from X to a point.

This paper establishes conditions for certain Markov processes to possess a unique, exponentially converging quasi-stationary distribution, especially in cases where the process exhibits identifiability properties. The conditions we've derived encompass those found in the literature for irreducible Markov processes and can be applied more broadly to processes with weaker assumptions, such as state space divisibility without full irreducibility. Our work also covers certain L\'evy processes and diffusion processes, including those on compact manifolds. A key aspect of our approach involves introducing a new concept of $\mathcal{L}_p$-identifiability and utilizing backward and forward Kolmogorov operators to analyze quasi-stationary behavior.

This study examines how changes in the chemical potential of graphene affect the positions of particles within a nanotube channel. Graphene's chemical potential is adjusted through the application of a gate voltage in simulations that model a device called a graphene nanodevice. These simulations, conducted with a molecular dynamics algorithm, reveal that altering the chemical potential results in dielectric particles moving away from the graphene surface and towards the center of the nanotube channel. Furthermore, the study observes that these particles accumulate near the central point due to electrostatic forces and organize into stable, equilibrium configurations.

This study aimed to explore the outcomes of patients treated in Emergency Departments based on the duration of their initial visit. The analysis utilized electronic health records from a large healthcare system, featuring a randomized design in which every half hour increment in initial treatment time served as the treatment. The results revealed several significant patient outcomes influenced by the duration of initial treatment, including a 0.8 percentage point increase in 30-day revisit rates and a 0.8 percentage point increase in readmission rates for patients whose initial treatment time was 30 minutes longer. Furthermore, patients experiencing longer initial treatment times had higher all-cause hospital readmission rates within 30 days (a 1.3 percentage point increase) and were more likely to experience adverse events following discharge (a 2.3 percentage point increase). The researchers discovered that certain diagnostic categories were more significantly impacted by variations in initial treatment time, including patients with primary diagnoses of infection, cardiovascular diseases, and neurological disorders. This study provides evidence that extending Emergency Department stay by just half an hour has a noticeable and statistically significant effect on patient outcomes, underscoring the need for timely treatment and non-intuitive consequences of treatment duration on patient health.

This study examines how a group of individuals with varying problem-solving abilities tackle a collective challenge where some require more effort than others, and it's been discovered that the distribution of difficulty levels significantly impacts their decision-making approaches. A shared threshold model was introduced, in which a parameter called the 'critical success rate' sets a minimum standard for success. Based on this threshold, scenarios emerged in which the group chose the most demanding task, the easiest task, or an intermediate level of challenge. A comprehensive numerical analysis was conducted to identify key factors influencing the decision-making process and to provide insights that could address real-world applications, such as how to design tasks that balance individual preferences and overall success probabilities in collective decision-making.

We investigated how background effects related to local charge conservation impact the measurement of charge-dependent correlations from collision data. Using digital simulations of minimum bias PbPb collisions at 2.76 TeV and pp collisions at 7 TeV, we examined the effects of these backgrounds on basic properties such as flow coefficients and subevent multiplicities. Our research indicates that specific background effects are relevant to particular measurements of charge-dependent correlations. Consequently, we suggest removing only the irrelevant background effects to minimize biases in experimental analyses.

This study offers a thorough examination of crowdfunding success from the crowd's perspective. Integrating insights from social psychology, statistics, and machine learning, we analyzed data from Kickstarter involving 10,000 projects. We found that crowd dynamics exhibit a level of complexity similar to individual project and creator characteristics. By employing machine learning and statistical techniques, we identified the crowd's influence on project funding and developed a predictive model to estimate project success and funding amounts. Comparing the crowd's impact to other project features, we determined that it plays a more significant role in predicting outcomes. Furthermore, our results indicate that crowd features outperform more traditional machine learning techniques, such as text analysis and deep learning, in predicting project success.

This study examines the application of federated learning to its purest form in real-world scenarios, specifically in the context of network intrusion detection.  With a strong emphasis on processing sensitive data within isolated local environments, we investigate how the novel FL approach can balance the needs of collaborative data utilization for collective benefit while maintaining individual data privacy.  Notably, our research showcases a practical representation of this concept through the implementation of federated intrusion detection systems.  This is achieved by combining LabVIEW and Python in a collaborative setup, where each partner has control over their local data and processing, despite sharing capabilities to detect and correct common attacks via collective experience and adjustments to shared models.  To illustrate the efficacy of this method, we present a concrete example involving the classification of KDD Cup 99 data.

The increasing complexity of robotic applications necessitates rapid task processing, which traditionally incurs a considerable time gap between task initiation and commencement. This research introduces a novel, efficient algorithm to expedite task launch times on robotic systems, focusing on ground vehicles. By differentiating between dependent and independent tasks, our algorithm optimizes task processing to run concurrently upon completion, thereby minimizing idle times during launch phases. Key features of our approach include: (1) identifying dependency relationships between tasks; (2) grouping independent tasks to launch simultaneously; and (3) launching a subset of dependent tasks simultaneously as soon as possible, based on the latest completion time of their preceding tasks. We further present a straightforward method to establish an optimal offline schedule as a baseline comparison. Through both theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation, our algorithm is demonstrated to achieve near-optimal performance in terms of processing time, with only a negligible processing overhead.

This research explores the performance limitations of a specific type of metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors, focusing on high electron mobility, driven by an understanding of the unique interface characteristics between the gate and semiconductor materials. Using a computational model, it was discovered that using aluminum or aluminum alloys for the gate results in a more stable and efficient oxide layer when combined with low workfunction gate materials, such as titanium or aluminum, and n-type semiconductor materials like germanium or silicon. However, this stability comes at the cost of increased scattering and electron effective mass, which in turn limits the maximum attainable mobility. Notably, it was found that using aluminum or aluminum alloys with high workfunction materials like hafnium oxide leads to higher carrier effective masses and thus lower maximum mobilities compared to traditional titanium or aluminum gate materials.

Our research examines the group synchronization of large networks composed of oscillators where system parameters exhibit minor fluctuations. Using a combination of theoretical analysis and experimental evidence from coupled rock-ing chairs, we investigate how these parameter deviations impact the stability of synchronized groups. Our findings reveal that even slight variations can significantly reduce the stability of synchronized groups, enabling the consolidation of smaller groups into larger ones. Nonetheless, we also identified a critical parameter range within which synchronized groups remain intact despite minor fluctuations.

Our study examined how prominent Western search engines respond to inquiries about YouTube, as the video platform is owned by a different company. We found that YouTube rarely appears in the search results provided by Google, Bing, and Yahoo, yet frequently appears in the output of Baidu, a Chinese search engine. Notably, in Baidu's search results, YouTube is often ranked higher than its official alternative, YouTube Music. We also found that Baidu's inclusion of YouTube may compromise its overall safety and reliability. Our analysis highlights the complexities of how different search engines address subdomain queries, touching on factors like censorship, credibility, and the influence of their respective owners.

This study introduces a novel extension to the $\beta$-function that incorporates the effects of various monodromy defects in 4D $\mathcal{N}=1$ super Yang-Mills theories, their coupled systems and associated dual descriptions. The investigation employs the lens of holographic duality in supergravity to derive the theory-based $\beta$-function extension. Additionally, the analysis examines the implications of mass-dependent and mass-independent deformations by superconformal $\beta$-functions.

Over a cubic Galois extension of rational numbers, we are examining specific elliptic curves that have a $K$-rational point of order 13. These points are then used to define a structure in a cubic extension that mirrors the structure of a supersingular elliptic curve over rational numbers, with a Tor-independent degeneration occurring when the order of the point reaches 13. For such curves with a $K$-rational point of order 13, we establish that the reduced specific height $\overline{h}_K$ of the elliptic curve is directly linked to the discriminant of the cubic extension, with this relationship being highly dependent on the properties of the extension and the position of the point. Utilizing this relationship, we are able to establish a lower bound on the reduced specific height of such curves in the event of a particular condition regarding the cubic extension and the point satisfying a specific criterion.

The temporal evolution of network protocols is affected by both spatial and temporal delays, which can be utilized to derive useful criteria for analyzing protocol dynamics. By examining the distribution of delays at various scales, this study identifies four operation modes - timely, near-timely, spread-out, and slow - which are characterized by distinct spatial and temporal delay ratios. A generic protocol is studied to illustrate how its behavior changes across these different operation modes, and a well-known delay-bounded consensus protocol is also used to demonstrate the applicability of these modes to real-world scenarios.

Semi-supervised node classification in graph neural networks often employs pseudo-labeling to enhance performance with limited labeled data. Current pseudo-labeling methods, which assign labels to unlabeled nodes based of labeled ones, can limit the node's potential to learn new information. To address this issue, we introduce a new pseudo-labeling technique that allows nodes to be labeled independently, without relying on labeled nodes, and utilize a new loss function to maintain class balance. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional pseudo-labeling methods, such as self-training and deep self-consistency, and achieves superior performance on four benchmark datasets.

Our proposed model, PatchNet, is a lightweight convolutional network designed specifically for efficient semantic video object detection. Built on the foundation of MobileNetV2, PatchNet leverages a novel framework that combines efficient feature extraction and aggregation across spatiotemporal dimensions. Unlike traditional models, PatchNet's architecture comprises a series of spatial and temporal block modules, enabling the extraction and pooling of local features, respectively. Consequently, this framework enables PatchNet to outperform other state-of-the-art models, including MobileNetV2, while reducing their computational complexity by 30-50%. Notably, PatchNet's performance surpasses other efficient backbones by a significant margin on KITTI and KIT3D datasets in terms of ADOR score, achieving a 10-20% improvement.

Recent research has focused on analyzing the multi-point distribution at discrete time points for a model called the discrete time TASEP, specifically with initial conditions that favor either large particles or empty spaces. This work builds upon that of Arous and Bercovici, who established an asymptotic formula for a related probability distribution in the context of independent random variables. Our results demonstrate that, even with more complex initial conditions, the multi-point distribution at discrete time points can be approximated asymptotically, leading to a formula that includes a log-singular-integral term.

This study investigates an hybrid SWIPT network that utilizes a mixed-integer nonconvex optimization approach to achieve energy efficiency in the long-term. The optimization problem aims to maximize the base station's power transfer to the users and minimize battery charging power, while satisfying power constraints and ensuring a minimum received power rate by each user. To resolve this problem, we derive an equivalent convex optimization issue with an equivalent convex form, and apply the Charnes and Cooper and Cramer's methods to yield a feasible solution. The resulting solution has a computational tractability issue as the number of users increases, hence we propose an alternative algorithm using an iterative approach to address this limitation. The simulation outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods.

We've developed a new perturbation theory for SU(N) fermions by applying a kernel approach to the interaction, and we've found that with an appropriate choice of kernel, the theory has purely analytical second-order and third-order results. Notably, the kernel's properties allow it to mimic the characteristics of various known interaction kernels, including the Gross-Neveu and Yukawa kernels. In third-order, the theory incorporates both a kernel-dependent and kernel-independent correction. In the SU(N) limit, the third-order kernel-dependent correction matches the perturbative QCD result for N=3, and when applied to the Gross-Neveu kernel, yields the perturbative QCD result for N=∞. We've also found that the third-order kernel-independent correction contains a mass-dependent term that matches the perturbative QCD result for N=3, and a ratio of loop integrals that appears in the SU(N) limit with N=∞.

In the quantum regime, the interaction between light and mechanical elements can be described by a quantum circuit network, even when the occupation numbers are significantly high. This is because the quantum description remains valid for any state configuration. By converting the optomechanical system into an electrical circuit, we can analyze the quantum-squeezed states of the mechanical oscillator, as well as the radiative field, using only classical signal processing techniques. These analyses rely on the correlations between the outputs of the circuit components, similar to conventional frequency-domain measurements. Notably, we find that the quantum squeezing of the mechanical oscillator corresponds to an anti-proportional relationship between the amplitudes of the mechanical and electrical signals processed in the circuit.

On the nonclassical Lommel polynomials of the second kind, two generalized weights - the generalized sextic Freud weight and the generalized Airy weight, each expressed as a product of powers of $x^n$ and $e^{cx^m}$, varying with $n$, $c$, $m$ and $k$, where $k$ is a nonnegative integer, with the former having a constant ratio of $c$ to the exponent's power, equal to $\frac{2}{m}$, is investigated. It is proven that the generalized sextic Freud weight leads to a monotone increasing sequence of natural numbers, in contrast to the unbounded nature of the generalized Airy weight, allowing for the derivation of strong asymptotic formulas for monic polynomial norms, similar to those seen in classical weights, as the degree of the polynomial increases without bound.

This research investigates how a robot that navigates by following walls, which senses its surroundings with a range-finding sensor, behaves in a situation where the sensor's field of view is limited. The study uses a simplified model to derive a key feature of the sensor's output, which influences the robot's movement trajectory. The analysis shows that the robot's trajectory is highly dependent on the sensor's field of view. The study provides a mathematical expression that characterizes the robot's speed and follows-distance under steady-state conditions, highlighting the sensor's impact and including a parameter that represents the sensor's accuracy.

We've investigated the structure of perturbative algebraic quantum field theory using a method that allows the use of any Cauchy surface for defining subalgebras, rather than being limited by spatial isometries. Our method involves using a rescaled interaction, which makes all local subalgebras zero. Our work focuses on examining the subalgebra structure on spacelike and timelike Cauchy surfaces of class C^1. We've established the subalgebra structure for a perfect fluid model of gravity and for Branson-rotation invariant theories.

A novel approach for training a smoke detection model is proposed, specifically designed to identify smoke in cluttered surgical environments. The method recognizes that manually labeling images is an impractical task due to the challenge and time-consuming nature of accurately categorizing images. To overcome this, the model utilizes a semi-supervised technique that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data for training. Furthermore, the method employs a dataset balancing algorithm to address class imbalance issues. To evaluate the model's effectiveness, it was tested on three datasets with contrasting characteristics. Compared to a baseline model, which relied on labeled data only, the proposed method achieved improved accuracy in detecting smoke. Specifically, the results showed enhanced performance on two datasets, while matching the performance on the third.

This study adapts the concept of frequency resilience from optical systems to superconducting qubits, applying it to design robust Molmer-Sorensen gates within threshold-based quantum processors. By leveraging a method to create nearly identical driving fields, the need for precise individual qubit frequency control is minimized, thereby increasing the frequency robustness of the gates. The research develops a framework to incorporate this method into a proven entanglement-accumulation strategy. As a result, a significant reduction is achieved in the minimum required entanglement cutoff for multi-qubit operations, thereby extending the practical application of such gates within threshold-based quantum processors.

A thorough investigation of the static distortions within perovskite structures has been conducted, focusing on the effects of A and B cations, as well as the equilibrium volume of the crystal. Our findings reveal the significance of the A cation size and equilibrium volume in determining the B cation's displacement pattern, with smaller A cations tending to cause B cation shifts in the [001] direction and larger A cations tending to cause shifts in the [110] direction. Additionally, the study found that the choice of B cation primarily influences the displacement distance, with larger B cations tending to cause increased distortion. An analysis of the bond lengths within the octahedra revealed that the B cation radius has a dominant effect, with the A cation size having a minimal but positive impact on this bond length variation.

We introduce a multivariate Gaussian process ensemble that maintains conditional independence between individual processes within the ensemble. This property enables us to represent the ensemble as a graphical model, where interactions between data streams are non-existent. This methodology has implications for machine learning and data analysis, particularly in situations where conditional independence between data streams is non-negotiable. For instance, forecasting and data analysis involving independent data streams - like stream data - pose challenges where conventional models fall short. However, with the multivariate Gaussian process ensemble, we can construct a matrix-valued GP such that its marginal distributions are univariate Gaussian processes, thereby ensuring conditional independence between individual processes within the ensemble. Furthermore, this methodology allows for the representation of interactions between data streams as a directed acyclic graph, where absent edges indicate true conditional independence. We develop methods for inferring and performing inference on these multivariate ensembles from a given joint Gaussian distribution. To facilitate their practical use, we introduce a variational inference algorithm that efficiently handles large datasets. This methodology is then applied to a stream forecasting problem involving the prediction of multiple time-series data streams simultaneously.

By integrating a two-step process involving wave function generation and property evaluation, ab initio quantum embedding achieves complete wave functions with minimal dependence on a smaller, embedded region. Wave function generation is typically handled through propagation in a forward manner, but property evaluation often demands a backward pass that involves computing the time derivative of the Hamiltonian and other operators. Previous wave function embedding schemes have incorporated these operators into the Hamiltonian to simplify the embedding process, but this approach introduces an artificial termination condition at the boundary between the embedded region and the surroundings. Our proposed method, called the multistep recursive quantum embedding method (MRQEM), eliminates these issues by separating the Hamiltonian and other operators and incorporating them only within the embedded region. MRQEM also utilizes a kicked interaction, allowing these operators to be applied over a brief time interval. As a result, the method excels at obtaining ground state properties while minimizing the impact of negative imaginary parts, a common issue in wave function embedding. MRQEM's efficiency and effectiveness are demonstrated through calculations on a series of small molecular systems.

A polynomial-time method called the Generalized Chebyshev method achieves optimal average-case efficiency compared to gradient descent for a broad range of non-convex objectives defined by a parameter $\kappa$. This algorithm combines principles from Chebyshev polynomials and a non-parametric optimization technique known as the Yuryev method. The Generalized Chebyshev method can be applied to various non-convex optimization problems, including those with occluded data access and equal expected costs. Its average-case performance is comparable to that of gradient descent on smooth, $\kappa$-strongly convex functions and $\kappa$-strongly convex functions with Lipschitz continuous Hessian, although it exhibits better worst-case performance in some scenarios. Additionally, the algorithm outperforms other known optimization methods, and its convergence rate is independent of the parameter $\kappa$.

Our research focuses on interlayer excitons in two specific moiré heterostructures, obtained by combining TBMT/TDMT and TBMT/HSMT materials. Using many-body perturbation theory incorporated in GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation, we accurately predict the interlayer exciton states and their associated spectra. We find that interlayer exciton transitions produce distinctive optical signals within a 20 meV energy range, which are significantly influenced by the interlayer exciton binding energy. This binding energy is strengthened by the moiré pattern's indirect hoppings, which are absent in monolayer materials. Moreover, our results show that the character of the interlayer exciton changes gradually from equally shared to primarily being localized on the lower layer as the energy increases.

This study introduces a novel adaptive probabilistic data association algorithm designed to minimize the impact of a mobile agent's momentum on position estimation in rapidly changing environments. The agents' states are represented by a Gaussian distribution, which is updated using a Bayesian filter, specifically the adaptive measurement update and predictive update method. The associated algorithm utilizes multiple hypothetical agents to account for the effects of the agent's velocity, which is also taken into account in the data association metric. The algorithm's performance is evaluated and compared with that of the standard probabilistic integration method under various conditions.

Initial findings from the analysis of the angular distributions of $W$ and $Z$ boson decays, influenced by their respective spins and polarization states, have been obtained using the LHCb experiment's complete 2011-2012 data set with integrated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$. The joint helicity fractions for $W$ and $Z$ bosons have been directly measured for the first time, and these results align with Standard Model predictions. The study also yields constraints on left-handed and right-handed $b \to c W^{-}Z$ and $b \to c W^{+}Z$ transition vertices, and these constraints will have significant implications for future searches for new physics in similar $b$-quark decays at other collider experiments.

A conformal transformation within Einstein gravity theory is utilized to link a non-conformally flat vacuum's Cotton tensor to the conformally flat vacuum's Ricci tensor, ultimately resulting in the Cotton tensor vanishing for the vacuum state in de Sitter space. Consequently, this implies that general relativity's de Sitter vacuum is a conformally coupled state. Similarly, the Cotton tensor is found to be zero for the vacuum state in anti-de Sitter space, suggesting that general relativity's anti-de Sitter vacuum is also a conformally coupled state. Furthermore, the fourth-order Einstein equations can be reduced to the second-order equations by performing a conformal transformation and utilizing the Cotton tensor equation, thereby retaining the degrees of freedom in the original theory.

We demonstrate that every orthomodular lattice is equivalent to a orthomodular space, providing a specific example of such a space in the form of a lattice of subspaces within a certain type of vector space.

This paper introduces ARP, a system that creates proof outlines in the F-logic format by combining query modification with proof generation. ARP's approach involves transforming natural language queries into F-logic patterns, which are then used to generate proof representations. We demonstrate the benefits of ARP by showcasing its ability to produce accurate proof outlines for complex semantically annotated datasets, such as knowledge graph datasets. We also explore the potential applications of ARP, such as incorporating its output into existing knowledge graph editing platforms, and provide an example of its utility in reviewing semantic changes made to TGCourses${^+}$.

We combine Watson's formula with recent moments calculations by Soundararajan and Harper to derive a broad inequality for the second moment of $L$-function coefficients within a critical interval. This generalization retains the sharp character of its underlying formulas.

A widely used approach for solving convex optimization problems, interior point methods, involves a sequence of iterations combining both outer and inner steps. The inner steps resolve a subproblem using a differentiable merit function, and it's common for these inner iterations to be part of a larger sequence where the inner subproblems become progressively simpler. This insight suggests an early termination strategy, where if the improvement per inner iteration drops below a certain threshold, further inner iterations can be skipped, saving computational time without significant additional expense. The proposed strategy can be applied in both primal and dual formulations and also extends to other algorithms with a similar inner structure, and our test cases with standard optimization problems indicate a substantial speedup when employing early termination.

To maintain the QCD asymptotic freedom within the variable flavor number scheme, a transition function $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ is defined, allowing for the transition from using $N_{f}=2$ to $N_{f}=3$ flavors in QCD perturbation theory. We derive the next-to-leading order (NLO) analytic expression for $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ and verify its accuracy through comparison with NLO-perturbative and numerical results. Additionally, an all-order match condition is formulated to obtain the next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) behavior of $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ and relevant parameters are calculated to determine the QCD coupling $\alpha_s(N)$ at $N=4,5$.

The AI Incident database documents real-world incidents that have been classified as AI-related failures. It serves as a resource to help researchers learn from these incidents and prevent similar problems arising in the development of intelligent systems. Currently, the database contains 126 reported incidents from 75 sources, and we've analyzed these in the context of the current AI landscape and 19 years of previous AI research. Our investigation reveals patterns and root causes across these incidents, and we suggest potential solutions to mitigate similar problems in the future.

A refined version of the Ernst equation, known as the ERG, includes a differential equation suitable for Yang-Mills theory in a curved spacetime context. The ERG equation ensures gauge invariance and includes a curvature-based vector field, which is useful for describing gravitational effects. The ERG equation's accuracy depends on the higher-order derivative terms and the choice of gauge. A specific solution to the ERG equation for a charged black hole in Yang-Mills theory was presented.

This paper introduces a monitoring system capable of identifying and resolving conflicts between multiple process definitions during actual operation. Upon detecting a conflict, the system generates a counteraction strategy to rectify the situation, taking into account the optimal course of action given the current process state and desired final state.

We have developed a protocol, Proto-Quipper-M, for designing quantum circuits that resemble the original Quipper circuit but operate on a different architecture. This protocol involves modifying a given circuit to work within the constraints of a Microsoft-specific quantum device. In the process, we've established a method to preserve the quantum nature of input states even after the circuit's completion, all while ensuring that additional measurements don't violate the principles of quantum mechanics. Proto-Quipper-M has been successfully tested with various circuits and devices to convert its outputs into a form compatible with the IBM quantum experience.

We analyze the statistical distribution of the largest eigenvalue near its upper critical point in three different random-matrix models: Ginzeau's ensemble, the Gaussian ensemble, and Sokolov's ensemble. By employing numerical methods at a comprehensive scale, our research reveals that these distributions conform uniformly to a universal form characterized by power-law behavior. The findings of this study substantiate theoretical predictions made in prior works (Kanzieper, Kuehn, and Suzuki [J. Phys. A 37, 3373 (2004)] and Kanzieper and Spohn [Phys. Rev. Lett. 93, 207201 (2004)]).

We investigate the principles behind quantum-enhanced sensing of an optical phase using two-mode squeezing. Our theory accurately predicts the sensitivity limits of such a system by considering key parameters, including the input photon count, squeezing parameter, and efficiency. We demonstrate that in practice, the level of two-mode squeezing achieved can significantly impact the minimum detectable phase angle. Our study further explores the trade-offs involved in the sensing process and the benefits of incorporating classical enhancement methods to achieve optimal performance.

One of the most challenging tasks in bioinformatics is reconstructing a long, contiguous sequence from shorter, overlapping fragments of DNA. As the size and number of these fragments increase, solving this problem becomes increasingly difficult, making it important to adapt and improve existing protocols for genome assembly. By generalizing the concept of number partitioning to multiple dimensions, researchers have created an efficient approach to genome assembly, outperforming traditional methods that work with single-dimensional numbers. Extensive testing with various genomes, ranging from small to several million base pairs in length, has demonstrated the significant speed and performance advantages of this new approach, making it suitable for most genomic sequences.

In a corresponding paper, the author proved a fundamental outcome for a modified logistic model with delay, and this note presents an alternative proof of that result using a different approach. The approach taken involves ensuring the non-existence of limit cycles in a system of two interconnected differential equations with a strictly increasing sign function and a delayed variable in one equation, and demonstrating that the system converges to a positive equilibrium.

Event times in competitive scenarios, such as neuronal interactions and online advertising, follow a point process dynamics where events occur at varying intervals. To compare these intervals effectively, a suitable transformation is needed to ensure they can be meaningfully compared and combined into a unified metric. The Isometric Log-Ratio transformation offers a powerful tool for doing so, with the ability to improve analysis accuracy and enhance statistical power. We've adapted ILR to fit point process data, ILR++ for inter-event intervals, and demonstrated its applications and benefits through simulations and real-world data sets.

In hybrid quantum conductors composed of a normal metal and a superconductor, linked by a interface, entangled Cooper pairs facilitate non-ballistic transport and generate spin-polarized quasiparticles. This research focuses on a four-terminal setup with an electrical current entering a normal metal contact and splitting between two superconducting leads. By examining spin-resonance absorption in this configuration, we have determined that entangled spin-triplets transmitted from the superconductors through the interface contribute significantly to this effect, potentially exceeding the influence of pure spin-polarized quasiparticles by a factor.

The isotope production of $^{66}$Ge was successfully achieved via the reaction $^{78}$Kr + $^{48}$Ti at an energy of 120 MeV, using the HI-13 cyclotron at the University of Mainz. The experiment was conducted with a high efficiency Si detector array consisting of 44 segments and  27 LaBr3 detectors to study gamma-ray transitions and nuclear levels in $^{66}$Ge. The nuclear levels in $^{66}$Ge were identified through 1n, 2n, and 3n neutron removal experiments and were observed up to an excitation energy of 4.5 MeV. By comparing the nuclear structure of $^{66}$Ge with $^{61}$Ni at similar neutron numbers, it was found that $^{66}$Ge exhibits a more closed shell-like structure, whereas $^{61}$Ni displays a deformed structure. Additionally, the experiments provided information on the nuclear structure of $^{66}$Ge and its potential applications in geoneutrinos and nuclear medicine.

The IMS $Bho$ system's sensitivity was significantly enhanced to include extremely short-lived, under-neutron isotopes in a recent study. The 82Ne, 83Ne, and 83Na isotopes were measured with the $Bho$-IMS setup, which was calibrated over a wide beam energy range of 2-5 MeV and achieved impressive detection sensitivity with the reaction of a 82Se target bombarded with 18Ne at an energy of 42 MeV. The detection sensitivity was further refined through extensive statistical analysis and the identification of background interference. The analysis revealed highly influenced isomeric state yields in 82Ne and 83Ne as a result of proton and gamma-ray decays following the direct nuclear reaction. The analysis of 83Na's decay path revealed a half-life of 83.9 milliseconds and a collective angular momentum of 5.6 +/- 0.6.

We introduce U(1) gauge theory within the context of a specific class of normalizing flows known as U(1) gauge transformations. This allows us to incorporate gauge symmetries into these models. We can then establish a direct connection between the traditional gauge principle and the concept of maximizing variational entropy under specified constraints. This connection enables us to derive charged Langevin dynamics from a strictly invariant action with respect to gauge transformations. We show that the conventional charged Langevin dynamics can be obtained by discretizing the temporal dimension and incorporating finite spatial lattice volumes. Furthermore, we provide an exact expression for the time-correlation function of a Gaussian charged field configuration derived from Langevin dynamics.

This research focuses on enhancing text recognition within autonomous driving using a more efficient model. The current state-of-the-art model, RANSAC, relies on a rigid assumption about the camera's position and the imaged street, which is not always accurate. To address this, we propose a new model that accounts for both camera and street distortions. We also develop a new training method that incorporates real-world biases to improve the model's performance. Prior studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of using biased models for recognizing specific text formats. To take this further, we developed a method that automatically creates multiple biased models from a single training image and selects the best one based on the actual scene. Our model not only outperforms the traditional RANSAC method but also achieves better results with fewer iterations.

The purpose of this research is to provide a detailed analysis of top quark production at a middle-energy scale, utilizing data from proton-antiproton collisions collected by the CDF II detector at Fermilab. The researchers measured the cross-section of top quark pairs in association with additional jets, and found the results to be consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics in its perturbative form. Additionally, the study determined the probability distribution of the number of jets accompanying top quark pairs and the characteristics of these associated jets.

This paper presents a new testing approach that assesses a pathway's capacity to identify relevant genetic information from public databases. During a simulated testing process, the only information available to the pathway is the sample's genetic data and a set of query questions that need to be answered. Unlike traditional testing methods where database contents are included, our approach evaluates the pathway's ability to search for necessary information. To improve the testing's reliability, we developed a database content prediction model that generates likely contents for each public database. As a result, when the pathway is tested with our simulated data, it is often accompanied by the predicted database content, which enhances the testing's execution accuracy. Furthermore, we established a standardized framework for evaluating and comparing different testing and training scenarios on these types of genetic analysis pathways.

We've conducted the first in-depth examination of angular clustering statistics for 1.1-smm bright galaxies at 0.4 < z < 2.4 by using data from the LoTSS-HASSP survey. This involves measuring the galaxy density around a given point and how that density changes with angular separation, and how that changes with galaxy characteristics like stellar mass and redshift. By applying a theoretical model, we've estimated the galaxy bias and how mass distribution changes with the scale. Our results show that the galaxy bias and how mass distributes are consistent with the standard cosmological model and the mean galaxy density. When comparing our results to galaxy evolution simulations, we found no significant discrepancy in the predicted galaxy bias and how mass distributes. However, the data suggest a possible increase in the mass distribute at higher redshifts than predicted by the simulations.

We present a new algorithm for solving the rank-limited lasso problem in high-dimensional linear regression, where our approach converts the problem into a series of less complex tasks by utilizing adaptive sieving with a customized criterion. This method is both computationally efficient and scalable, thanks to the incorporation of a suitable oracle-based procedure in each sieving step. Under certain assumptions, our algorithm is shown to have optimal performance, specifically achieving a guaranteed error rate of O((s^r + s^2) / sqrt(n)), where s represents the sparsity level, r indicates the rank limitation, and n denotes the sample size, resulting in improved asymptotic performance compared to existing methods.

Building upon previous findings that the lowest entropy production rate occurs at the optimal communication protocol, this study confirms this phenomenon for any definition of protocol efficiency. The research demonstrates that the optimal protocol, achieving the minimum rate of entropy production, does not necessarily involve the optimal protocol for efficient communication. Unlike previous outcomes where the optimal protocol was unique, this study reveals that the optimal protocol for minimal entropy production is not uniquely defined. The work explores the conditions under which a unique optimal protocol exists and identifies a criterion related to the convexity of the entropy production function.

As artificial intelligence continues to evolve, its applications are becoming embedded in various sectors, driving widespread adoption across the globe. Despite its numerous benefits, the growing environmental impact of AI services is increasingly clear, necessitating an accurate assessment of their ecological effects. This study introduces a novel framework for evaluating the environmental footprint of AI model training, informed by real-world examples from the media and finance sectors. The framework's capabilities will enable businesses and organizations to accurately measure the environmental implications of their AI initiatives, facilitating more sustainable AI development and deployment practices.

Current process monitoring techniques primarily focus on descriptive analyses, leaving a significant gap in prescriptive methods that advise specific actions to mitigate problems ahead of time. To bridge this disparity, a new, pioneering approach in the field aims to recommend proactive, real-time interventions when an optimal course of action is known in advance. This innovative method was developed within the process mining framework and has been implemented in a democratic decision-making process. To ensure its effectiveness and validity, it underwent testing in two distinct process scenarios. One of these scenarios involved simulated cases, while the other involved a real-world application in a Finnish Parliament. The results of these tests not only validated the technique but also yielded valuable process improvements.

A novel, locally valid and reliable error estimate is developed for coupled problems of fluid dynamics without power. The estimate draws on a dual-weighted residual method, requiring only the solution of an auxiliary problem with similar characteristics to the primary problem. The estimate can be utilized as an indicator for adaptive mesh refinement, enhancing solution precision with reduced mesh size. The efficacy of this error estimate is demonstrated on a range of complex coupled fluid models, encompassing Stokes-Hamilton-Owen, Navier-Stokes-Brinkman and Navier-Stokes-VOF equations.

Graph packing problems have been a significant focus for many years, with numerous applications across various fields including network design and scheduling. In a graph packing problem, a set of subgraphs or specific structures are selected and combined within a given graph, adhering to certain overlap and connectivity requirements. Although various upper bounds have been developed for these problems, tight bounds remain elusive, particularly for complex variants such as vertex-disjoint paths. In this study, we introduce a new approach to derive more precise upper limits for certain graph packing problems by employing linear programming. We apply this method to two specific challenges: finding vertex-disjoint cycles and long vertex-disjoint paths in graphs, and present improved bounds for both.

In a system where agents have one-dimensional opinions, their interactions and occasional swapping of opinions can result in the emergence of social groups. Even without the influence of comprehensive information, opinions are organized into distinct segments. Our primary goal is to examine how these groups develop and the rules they follow, starting from an evenly distributed opinion structure among agents. We also investigate how these groups change in response to external circumstances, such as the arrival of new agents.

Our analysis focuses on a four-dimensional $\mathbb{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory coupled with a scalar field, which is a modification of the Weiberg-Wise model. This setup is equivalent to a five-dimensional black hole equation with asymptotically flat boundaries. Our findings reveal that the model exhibits scalar black holes with two independent solutions, which are analogous to the normal and superconducting states in holographic superconductors. In the superconducting regime, the scalar field's decay at the event horizon mirrors the Meissner effect, and the black hole's spin is directly proportional to its charge. Furthermore, in the superconducting regime, the temperature's upper bound is directly proportional to the inverse of the chemical potential, and multiple values of the potential can correspond to a single upper bound of the temperature.

The process of producing a mature mRNA from a transcript involves several steps following transcription completion: initiation of initiation delay, initiation of splicing, processing, and final polyadenylation. Our model, the "train model," describes how the length of a gene influences the delay between transcription completion and the production of mature mRNA. The train model indicates that the total delay is directly proportional to the length of a gene. This linear relationship explains why, despite variations in gene length, the delays are generally similar. The train model also predicts that changes in processing rates or initiation delays will result in corresponding changes in production times. Our model does not address the causes of these similarities and disparities, but it provides a framework for understanding how different processes contribute to the overall production time of a mature mRNA.

The paper discusses the findings from a high-precision, isotope-based research on the 64Ni nucleus, focusing on its response to excitations. The measurements, carried out using the 64Ni target with various isotopes of nickel, were complemented by first-principles calculations. The researchers analyzed the excitation energy distribution and response patterns across different energy domains to understand the 64Ni nucleus. The data showed a significant subshell gap at N = 40, which drives the nucleus's collective behavior. The measurements revealed a substantial monopole interaction that governs the nucleus's shape and excitation patterns. The data also showed that 64Ni has a prolate deformation and multiple collective excitations, which were correctly predicted by calculations. The study provides a thorough understanding of the 64Ni nucleus and its behavior, shedding light on its structure and the subshell gap at N = 40.

We're studying an SU(N) gauge theory that includes additional Weyl fermions, represented in the adjoint and fundamental representations. By adding more Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation, the theory generates a family of (2N-1)2 and (2N+1)2 anomalies for SU(N) with N greater than or equal to 3. When we add Weyl fermions in the fundamental representation, the theory generates a family of (2N-1)2 and (2N+1)2 anomalies for SU(N) with N greater than or equal to 3, as well as linearly dependent (2N+1)2 and (2N-1)2 anomalies. Our results align with the predictions made by Kidney and Aharony in their paper titled "Anomalies and the Periodic Table of Elementary Particles" and support their proposal that certain elements in the periodic table of particles and solitons can be derived from the properties of supersymmetric quiver theories.

We establish the equivalence between the group codes $C$ and $D$, and their dual codes $D^{\perp}$, using a specific decoding algorithm that first applies a known decoding method for $C$ and then uses the group action of $C$ to correct additional errors in $D^{\perp}$. This technique allows us to prove the equivalence without needing information about a specific right inverse of the covering map $\pi: D \rightarrow C$.

Bucket Elimination, a variable elimination method on directed acyclic graphs, is enhanced by various on-the-fly and offline adaptations. These adaptations accelerate inference and optimization tasks, but come with a cost: increasing computational time as the removal of variables and their associated cliques progress. In this research, we introduce a new BUE algorithm that overcomes this limitation while maintaining constant time complexity. This advancement applies to any BUE adaptation, including but not limited to, propagating logarithmic potentials and optimizing linear submodular functions. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical efficacy of our findings through relevant experiments.

This paper presents a unified approach to detecting dropped objects in various settings. Our method integrates knowledge from multiple disciplines to design a single framework that can be adapted for multiple domains. This integration draws from psychology, robotics, and machine learning to effectively combine sensory inputs and model agent behavior. We develop a key concept of 'event impact severity' to standardize responses across diverse domains and evaluate its effectiveness through simulation tests.

Research on jamming transitions in two-dimensional systems has been expanded by exploring the effects of different types of friction. A theoretical and numerical study has identified a distinct jamming transition caused by friction, distinct from the isotropic jamming transition. The study also found that the exponents governing this transition vary significantly depending on the type of friction and the order parameter used. In contrast to the isotropic jamming transition, which has exponents close to those in percolation, the frictionally induced jamming transition has a first-order character, as evidenced by a lack of power-law behavior in the compressibility and force autocorrelation times. The study further reveals that even minor anisotropy resulting from friction significantly alters the jamming transition for directionally dependent order parameters, leading to a transition order, as evidenced by the divergence of such parameters with decreasing contact radius.

A proposed model, MS(2)-AR(4), combines the memory in multivariate time series with the flexibility of autoregressive components, outperforms the standard AR model when time series have inherent structure.
