This limit can be expressed as the product of the de-Broglie wavelength and the surface area, or less, expressed through the curvature radius and the Euler characteristic of the space.

We have introduced a novel complex-valued version of affine coupling layers that can be utilized in Monte Carlo simulations, and we have derived the condition under which they behave as traditional coupling layers. This derivation, combined with the Lancaster--Zhang--Sohl-Dickstein--Arden--Madigan bound, enables us to establish a practical threshold for determining the number of coupling layers required in a simulation. In addition, we have developed a method for efficiently sampling from complex distributions, and we have tested its efficacy by applying it to both simple and complex scenarios.

We present a realistic model incorporating natural mass hierarchy and a substantial intergenerational mixing within the quark sector. The U(1)_F flavor symmetry is represented by U(1) in the spirit of Georgi-Pais and Dorsner et al., yet we've modified it to incorporate the anomalous U(1)_A and U(1)_Y symmetries for better consistency. By combining the elements of the Dorsner et al. and Barr model constructions, we generate a breaking pattern that matches the CKM data, with the exception of the lambda parameter which remains unsolved. The ratio of the top to bottom quark masses is significantly resolved. The model includes two heavy degrees of freedom, a pseudo Goldstone boson and a dark Dirac fermion whose interaction with the Higgs boson is kept minimal.

Virtual Private Networks have become essential for accessing the internet privately, but concerns are growing over their security in the face of increasing malware threats. A new type of malicious entity, the Virtual Private Network Malware (VPPM), has been identified and is expected to exacerbate existing cyber threats. Previous research focused on traditional VPNs and did not explore their virtual counterparts. This study aims to identify and analyze the characteristics of VPPMs through a proposed detection method. A new reference dataset, the Malicious Virtual Private Malware Signature Dataset, has been developed to support VPPM research. By comparing different machine learning algorithms, a five-layer neural network was found to be the most effective in detecting VPPMs. Furthermore, an investigation into the classification of highly malicious VPPM sub-classes was conducted. The outcome of this study will contribute to a better comprehension of the VPPM threat and aid in improving malware detection through the development of the Malicious Virtual Private Malware Classification Framework.

While large language models have achieved impressive results in natural language understanding, they are often limited to languages in their training data. This study investigates the requirements for a model to efficiently adapt to new languages in various tasks and finds that incorporating word and token-level information is essential. Additionally, the study examines how the number of new words and the model's size affect adaptability, discovering that with sufficient data, even small models can effectively learn new languages.

Research indicates that rotating core collapse initially follows a binary mass influenced pathway, with the ratio of kinetic to gravitational energy increasing in a roughly mass-dependent manner, although this ratio peaks earlier for more massive objects. Beyond this point, the ratio's decline indicates a transition from a roughly oblate to a more symmetric structure, with growing influence from magnetic forces, which can also make the collapse slower and more magnetic force-dominated in general, larger masses initially.

A modified version of the well-known k-means clustering method, known as the m-ar-K function, has been developed with the goal of improving dimensionality reduction techniques. This new approach is inspired by a modified version of the Euclidean distance metric, which retains the characteristics of its original counterpart with improved performance. When compared to traditional methods such as PCA or ICA, early tests have indicated that m-ar-K can achieve superior results in both classification and clustering tasks.

A proposed EPC (Extended Polynomial Calculus) for first-order logic with arithmetic operations may offer a more practical alternative to existing polynomial calculus. If a super-polynomial EPC lower bound holds, it could imply that PTIME is not closed under the CPT (Complement of Turing Machine) operation, a possibility that has significant theoretical and practical implications. Furthermore, the relationship between CPT and PTIME has far-reaching consequences for our understanding of the complexity of SAT, the satisfiability problem for Boolean formulas, as its hardness has been linked to fundamental questions in logic and model theory. A super-polynomial EPC lower bound for SAT would resolve long-standing open questions in logic and model theory, the low-down theorem and the extended down-up theorem, respectively.

A ring is $\sigma$-elementary if the ideals of one type have similar properties throughout the ring $\sigma(R)$. In this research, we examine a commutative ring with a monoid $\sigma$ set of permutations, and discover that for certain specific $\sigma$-elementary rings, an involutive permutation results in the ring being either purely power-commutative or anti-commutative. Additionally, we find that for certain specific $\sigma$-elementary rings with an involutive permutation, it is possible to define a commutative square anti-associative binary composition operation whose algebra is either purely power-associative or Malcev.

The prevalence of social media in everyday life has made it imperative to comprehend the diverse perspectives expressed on various issues, such as politics and medicine, in order to foster more informed discussions. The numerous posts on the internet present a significant challenge to deciphering the distinct viewpoints and their respective arguments. Although some studies focus on extracting opinion segments from text, there is a greater need to thoroughly grasp the underlying narratives that govern the expression of opinions in social media forums. To address this gap, we have developed a system that utilizes a two-stage process to both identify and interpret the narratives within social media posts. To achieve this, we first employ a narrative identification stage, where we leverage a pre-curated taxonomic system to classify posts into distinct categories. Subsequently, we utilize a variety of natural language processing techniques to pinpoint the specific phrases within each category that exemplify characteristic narrative arguments. To establish a baseline for our approach, we conducted an experiment limited to three topics: vaccine development, climate change, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The results of our experiment demonstrate the efficacy of our system in accurately categorizing posts and pinpointing narrative arguments compared to existing benchmark models.

This paper presents a novel approach to event detection that takes into account
temporal and spatial contexts across multiple cameras with varying resolutions.
A new model is developed to process video streams from these cameras, where each
event is defined by a distinct set of pixels on one sensor. The system utilizes
event timestamps and a corresponding density function to measure the
significance of each event occurring within a specified time frame. By
considering the event detection as a multi-dimensional problem, where each
dimension represents a different camera, the system calculates a unified metric
to evaluate the significance of each event. Finally, a method is developed to
determine the optimal set of events that best fit the data, where the significance
of each event is recalculated iteratively until convergence.

We've made the most accurate measurement to date of how galaxy distributions are affected by gravity and the universe's mass through a specific type of galaxy in the Clusius-Huygens cluster. To arrive at this conclusion, we analyzed data from a specific galaxy in the CHAOS-W4 cluster at a redshift of 0.27. To achieve this, we combined multiple approaches: examining an area of 20 by 20 arcminutes around the cluster center using a specific technique known as "lens or no lens" yielded an estimate that is consistent with the universe's mass distribution. To account for potential uncertainties, we also analyzed an area of 1.5 by 1.5 degrees around the cluster and considered a variety of assumptions surrounding galaxy clustering and dark matter. Our final results show that an area of 1.5 by 1.5 degrees around the cluster is the most accurate choice for analyzing these phenomena. Our findings provide the tightest constraints to date on the universe's mass distribution and the way galaxy distributions are affected by gravity, with our results being the most accurate to date.

We have devised a novel framework that provides robustness against significant data corruption for deep learning models by incorporating a worst-case scenario challenge during training. Unlike current approaches which focus on protecting against minor data tampering, our framework aims to safeguard against substantial and realistic data alterations. Our method involves including an adversarial component in the training data, where we utilize the BREEZE algorithm to find the most damaging perturbation and pair it with the original sample. This framework has been successfully applied to enhance the robustness of tabular data deep learning models and has shown superior performance in withstanding substantial data corruption compared to existing methods.

Our research investigates the dynamics of rumor spread across different times and locations, treating the spread process as a temporal and spatial correlation. We analyze how precursor information and other factors affect the peak and decline of rumors, using data from Weibo. Our findings indicate that the peak of a rumor is largely determined by its initial characteristics, while its decline is influenced by various location-specific factors. Consequently, creating targeted anti-rumor campaigns late in the spread process may have limited effects, but early campaigns that leverage local factors can help reduce the impact of a rumor.

Dimensionality reduction is a crucial initial step in many hyperspectral pixel classification techniques.  Among the various methods, such as PCA, ICA, and CCA, 
two self-guided approaches – Auto-Encoder and Guided Filter – have shown potential in enhancing signal reconstruction and classification performance. 
By integrating these methods, a new combined strategy is proposed to improve three types of dimensionality reduction techniques, resulting in more efficient 
classification results according to experimental data obtained from both simulated and real-world hyperspectral datasets.

Deep neural networks require substantial storage and computation resources, 
which has prompted the development of various methods for its efficient compression.
A novel two-stage framework is proposed to compress DNNs quickly and effectively.
Initially, a modified pruning technique is employed to substantially reduce the model's 
memory and computation requirements while minimizing performance loss.
Next, a proposed framework based on low-rank decomposition is used to further optimize 
the residual network structure, resulting in considerable fusion of weight matrices and 
reduced model size without affecting accuracy.
Experimental results show that this framework can achieve comparable accuracy to the 
original model with a reduction of over 90\% model size when tested on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

Protein structure prediction has made significant breakthroughs in recent years, 
mainly due to the incorporation of ab-initio folding simulations into the process.
However, current methods are not able to accurately utilize full ab-initio simulations 
as they require an inordinate amount of computational power.
  To address this limitation, a new approach called ProCS is presented, which effectively 
utilizes low-resolution structures produced by rapid ab-initio folding simulations 
as re-start points to significantly lower the energy barrier for further refinement.
  By combining ProCS with molecular dynamics and energy minimization, a comprehensive 
structure refinement method is achieved, which has been successfully validated through 
experiments on 105 test cases, showcasing improved performance over current best 
practices in structure refinement.

We're looking at supervised learning problems where the primary loss function isn't often used but still provides accurate predictions - specifically, KLDiv. Our investigation focuses on why this might be the case, and we identify two key reasons: minimization doesn't consistently train accurate models, and under-represented research hinders direct comparison of loss functions. To address these issues, we develop a method to accurately compare KLDiv with more common loss functions, and we show that, contrary to expectations, neither cross-entropy nor mean squared error perform as well as KLDiv. Moreover, we find that using KLDiv results in significantly better robustness against adversarial attacks.

The Hamiltonian-derived model of quantum field theory, a new approach to TQFT, is investigated in the context of 2D perturbative interactions.  By comparing the amplitude derived from the Hamiltonian with the standard parquet amplitude, it is found that the latter fails to satisfy key symmetries, specifically conservation and crossing symmetry, whereas the former does.  As a result, the latter cannot correctly describe these symmetries even at low orders of perturbation theory, despite agreeing with the former at the lowest order.

We conducted time-resolved angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (tr-ARPES) on monolayer TiSe2 to investigate the dynamics following laser excitation. Our results from directly observed spectral weight changes indicate the rapid emergence ($\sim$ 200 fs) and growth (over $\sim$ 1.8 ps) of a condensate related to an exciton, which competes with a charge-density-wave state. By combining tr-ARPES with ab initio density functional theory, we determined that the exciton condensation leads to significant retention of spectral weight at the Fermi level, whereas the charge-density-wave state results in a downward shift of the Fermi surface. Our findings support the concept that exciton condensation and charge-density-wave states are intimately connected in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides.

Emergency dispatch centers worldwide rely on text-based risk reporting systems to collect vital information from callers, which is then assessed to determine the level of response required. These systems have been the subject of numerous studies aimed at developing decision support tools, but there has been a lack of comprehensive data to inform the design of such systems. Our research gathered over 120,000 real-world incidents from eight dispatch centers in different countries, revealing the structure of these systems varies significantly depending on the type of emergency reported. While some common characteristics are shared, the data highlights the need for tailored dispatch systems to effectively support responders and improve safety.

The presence of superconductivity in materials with a Fermi surface that has a complex topology can lead to an anomaly in their magnetic susceptibility, which can be most notably observed in materials with a Fermi surface that has a hole electron zone that is nested with an electron hole zone. This nesting condition is crucial in the phase transition of high-Tc superconductors, particularly in the d(x,y) wave symmetry scenario, where the magnetic susceptibility exhibits a cubic divergence at the quantum critical point. To investigate this further, we have developed a theoretical framework that incorporates the effects of long-range ferromagnetic interactions in half-filled Hubbard models with an Ladder Hubbard model structure. Our findings indicate that an isotropic ferromagnetic interaction on the rungs of this type of lattice can drive a quantum critical point where the Fermi surface changes from a simple to a more complex topology. This complex topology is characterized by a zone with a spiral geometry that is separated by a gap from a adjacent electron hole zone. This spiral zone is born out of a folding of the electron hole zone as the ferromagnetic interaction strength increases. Furthermore, we have discovered that an isotropic ferromagnetic interaction on the rungs can drive a phase transition into an antiferromagnetic state that is coupled with a change in the Fermi surface topology. This change in the Fermi surface can be most notably observed in materials with a Fermi surface that has a hole electron zone that is nested with an electron hole zone. This nesting

Active learning algorithms designed for deep neural network classification tasks often assume that the network's output and ground truth are available for a labeled dataset, but the network's uncertainty and diversity in unlabeled data remain unaddressed. This paper presents a semi-supervised active learning method that incorporates entropy-based uncertainty and diversity considerations. Our approach, called Semi-Supervised Minimax Entropy-based Active Learning (SSMEL), involves a minimax game where a discriminator learns to distinguish between labeled and unlabeled data, and the generator, which is a classifier, is trained to maximize the discriminator's uncertainty. Since this process is constrained to maintain the labeled data's posterior probability. SSML enables the efficient selection of high-impact unlabeled data without relying on approximate models of the posterior. Our experiments demonstrate that SSML outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and semi-supervised active learning methods.

This research explores the evolution of song timbre from 1955 to 2015 across different genres, using features derived from spectrograms to identify decade-specific patterns in song similarity. A network of 11,862 popular songs was created, grouped by decade and genre, to analyze their inter-song similarity. The results show that songs within each decade and genre share distinct, persistent characteristics, despite dynamic changes in music trends. Additionally, the research reveals a significant increase in songs with similar traits over time, particularly in genres that emphasize live instrumental performance. By developing a method to link songs with similar traits across different genres and decades, the study identified recurring patterns in song similarity and identified 'father-son' relationships among artists, including connections between Ray Charles and Eric Church, and between James Brown and D'Angelo.

Consider an independent, identically distributed, zero-mean, bounded stochastic process (Yt, Rt) in R^d, where Yt represents the observed trajectory from time 0 to t, and Rt denotes a random variable indicating the time Yt becomes 'visible' or observable. We investigate stochastic processes that reward us when Yt becomes visible at time Rt. We explore both upper and lower bounds for the probability that the number of blocks in these processes within a given time period exceeds a certain threshold, where each block is defined as a segment of the process between two consecutive times it becomes visible. Our main finding shows that as time increases to infinity, the probability that the number of blocks in these processes exceeds a certain threshold converges to either zero or one, depending on whether that threshold is less than or greater than the expected number of blocks per unit time. We also establish conditions under the dependence regime where the process Yt, Rt is non-deterministic and has reinforcing properties, affecting the stochastic reward sequence.

Our Proof-Theoretic semantics aims to provide a transparent and intuitive meaning to formulas within sequent calculus, by focusing solely on the underlying natural deduction system with minimal additional concepts. The core of our semantics consists of three key elements: containment relationships, the converse relationship between principles, and the notion of redundancy. To formalize the first aspect, we introduce a 'less than' relation, enabling the definition of 'PT-semantics'. We then demonstrate that this semantics is equivalent to 'Cut-elimination' semantics for sequent calculus, a concept developed by Belnap. Regarding the converse relationship between principles, we show that it arises naturally from the cut rule within sequent calculus. Furthermore, the notion of redundancy is reflected in the fundamental cut principle.

Reward learning systems, which allow agents to learn optimal policies without explicit model assumptions, are reliant on a key feedback loop involving comparison of the agent's actions. The path to optimal policy deployment involves a series of comparisons, necessitating a large workforce for comparison of all possible actions. To optimize comparison requests from a limited workforce, we've developed a system to group and prioritize comparisons based on their relative effectiveness in advancing the learning process. The outcome is a significant decrease in the required comparisons to achieve the same level of performance as a fully-attended reinforcement learning trajectory.

The Smyth powerspace is a construction that maps a topological space to a space of subspaces of it,  where the topology is generated from a specific basis. It has the property that if the original space is core-compact, the resulting space will also be core-compact. However, this property holds only consistently for the Quasi uniform topology, in the context of smooth spaces. Smooth spaces are a type of core-compact space that includes compactly generated spaces and locales, and smooth locales are core-compact locales with a certain property. When applying the Smyth powerspace to a smooth locale, the resulting space may not be smooth. Nevertheless, research found that the Espinoza-Kelly powerspace, which is another construction for a topological space, when applied to a smooth locale, yields a smooth locale. Let's call this locale EK-smooth. The Espinoza-Kelly powerspace is different from the Smyth powerspace in that it maps a space to subspaces that have a specific property and whose intersections are also subspaces with that property. It was found that EK-smooth locales have a specific property and when applied to a compactly generated locale, the resulting space will also be compactly generated. However, not all compactly generated locales are smooth, and it was found that the Espinoza-Kelly powerspace adds a new property to some of these locales.

The behavior of vortex loops in a two-dimensional ideal fluid is examined in the context of a configuration space that is both three-dimensional and topologically equivalent to the complement of a plane in which the loops are situated. We are able to provide a precise description of how the configuration space's geometry changes as loops in the fluid's interior expand or contract, filling up a specific area they encircle. Furthermore, our study reveals that the configuration space exhibits a unique structure consisting of two parts: one which resembles the interior of a three-dimensional solid shape called a deltoid, and another component whose properties depend on the loops' interaction within that deltoid and the area they collectively encircle.

A popular AIPW approach is widely used for identifying causal relations in observational studies, especially when dealing with high-dimensional data. Although AIPW is often used with Lasso and its variants for both estimation and inference, our research shows that omitting the regularization that led to the initial sparse model results in a substantial decline in the performance of the AIPW test. To resolve this issue, we introduce a new approach that includes two main components: a return of centeral regularization terms in the AIPW estimator and the use of post-selection AIPW, yielding superior outcomes compared to existing methods.

The tau lepton, being heavy in comparison to light hadronic states, makes it ideal for lattice studies. This work focuses on the tau's mass, with results obtained using the Feynman-Hellmann theorem through various lattice observables, allowing for a quality check of the approach. Three independent methods were employed to determine the tau mass, and the differences between their outcomes were examined to assess systematic errors. Our final estimate for the tau mass is $1.7759(45)_{stat}(32)_{sys}$ MeV, and the quality of the lattice correlations between the tau's invariant mass and various observables was also evaluated.

We examine how baroclinic waves develop and behave in a rotating, horizontal cylinder with a vertically varying density of fluids, focusing on the surface and the boundary between the inner and outer layers. Using a theoretical approach, we determine the most dominant patterns of these waves and then numerically investigate how these patterns emerge and change over time. To gain a deeper understanding, we look at the energy within the system and the process by which it transfers from one layer to another, both as the patterns begin to form and as they reach a steady-state. We also consider how these layers interact and the effect of the rotating speed on the surface and internal dynamics of the system.

This study adapts Bayesian models from Heffernan and Tawn (2004) to address issues of extreme values, and proposes two methods for handling models with challenging computations. A method is developed to set the tuning parameter'm', which is currently set manually, and a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm is improved using a novel technique for accelerating mixing. Using simulated data and long-lasting observations, the methods are evaluated through various analyses, and evidence suggests they are effective.

In this paper, we explore a challenging reinforcement learning problem, considering a scenario where an agent interacts with a corrupt environment. The corruption is modeled through the parameter epsilon, which represents the probability that the agent receives incorrect feedback. We assume access to an oracle that can detect corruption with a high degree of certainty, yet, in practice, the extent of corruption, epsilon, remains unknown. To create robust algorithms that adapt to varying levels of corruption, we first establish a boundary on the optimal expected return under different corruption probabilities. Building upon this understanding, we design a meta-algorithm that efficiently handles corruption at different scales by leveraging a corpus of sub-optimal policies. The algorithm is then refined to estimate the corruption level and implemented in a series of policies that are resilient to corruption at different levels, outperforming existing methods in such scenarios.

The study focuses on the controllability of the impulsive heat equation, a nonlinear system influenced by sporadic and significant controls. The purpose of this investigation is to examine approximate controllability under large discrete controls and establish a limit process to achieve this goal. The solutions utilized involve a stochastic impulsive differential equation, highlighting a relationship between stochastic and deterministic control models. The findings are further generalized to apply to the fractional impulsive heat equation.

Detectors for identifying data that doesn't fit in with what a model has been trained on are crucial for responsible AI, but many of these detectors have been shown to fail when tested on data that's only slightly different from what a model was trained on. There's also a lack of agreement in the research community about what makes good out-of-distribution detection. To address these issues, we've come up with a set of tests that evaluate a detector's performance in a variety of scenarios and help us understand its strengths and weaknesses. These tests include detecting data with obvious flaws, subtle changes to existing data, and data from completely new distributions. We've used them to evaluate and compare different detection methods, and found that some of them perform surprisingly well on some tasks, but struggle with others. We hope these tests will help standardize the development of better detectors and make it clearer what characteristics they should have.

Motor proteins rely on Repulsion forces, triggered by electric currents, to overcome normal obstacles and maintain their forward movement. The electric currents that drive these repulsive forces also cause the motor's power stroke to accelerate its movement. The speed at which the motor progresses is determined by the balance between the electric drive and the energy released from ATP breakdown. The power stroke is typically controlled by a mechanical block or check valve that ensures the motor takes larger steps when the electric drive overcomes this barrier. The electric force can bypass this control mechanism, allowing the motor to take longer steps. We investigated the movement of kinesin-2, a dimeric molecular motor with two heads that progress on microtubules, under the influence of electric currents. Our research shows that electric currents can cause the motor to take longer steps by bypassing the blockage at its power stroke, leading to unusually long steps and irregular movement patterns. The electric currents also cause the motor to take larger steps when it is blocked, and this effect is more pronounced when the motor is stuck. The electric currents can also cause the motor to move backwards, especially when it is not blocked, and this effect increases at lower electric velocities. Our research suggests that electric currents can cause molecular motors to move in the opposite direction by increasing the duration of power stroke acceleration. The electric currents can also cause the motor to take longer steps by accelerating the power stroke while it is not blocked, and this effect is more pronounced at higher electric velocities. Our

A one-way word transducer with an origin label on the input word is called an origin-preserving one-way word transducer. This type of transducer maintains the starting point of the input word during processing. It can be shown that a non-deterministic two-way word transducer, when restricted to only use a finite number of space on its tape, has an equivalent but simplified form called a deterministic one-way word transducer in a specific context. This simplified form, however, may not always be available for all regular resynchronizers. In this research paper, a particular type of resynchronizer called bounded, regular resynchronizer is studied in depth. Using a specific property called image closure, it is demonstrated that any non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be replaced with an origin-preserving one-way word transducer, using a bounded, regular resynchronizer in the form of a sequence of consecutive states.

Our research delves into the efficiency of the f-Convolvolution, specifically its 36th iteration, which is known for its complex calculation typically requiring the full computation. We've found a method to calculate a single entry of the convolvolution much faster than computing the entire thing. This is made possible by a new generation function that allows for such a shortcut, and we're able to prove its correctness using a formal induction. Moreover, we identify key conditions under which this modified approach can be applied to earlier iterations of the convolvolution.

GJ 229B, a T/Y dwarf star located 18.8 light-years from the Sun in the constellation of Pavonis, was discovered in 1995 after an observational breakthrough using a 2.3-meter telescope at the Arizona-Steward Observatory. Prior to this, it was believed that planets and stars shared a clear dividing line, but GJ 229B's discovery along with TRAPPIST-1-e and the subsequent analysis of its properties revealed a grey area, known as intermediate objects, between the two. A 1999 study claimed that GJ 229B had a massive planet, but subsequent spectroscopic research appeared to contradict each other. A 2001 atmospheric model suggested that the surrounding atmosphere of GJ 229B could be responsible for the observed properties, but a ground-based spectroscopic study in 2010 raised new questions. A ground-based spectroscopic study in 2015 provided a precise measurement of GJ 229B's mass and size, but the mass was found to be higher than expected for a planet. A 2019 study using data from the Gaia spacecraft provided a precise measurement of GJ 229B's distance, but the mass was found to be higher than the 2015 study. A ground-based spectrographic study in 2020 discovered that GJ 229B had a massive disk, but the planet or star nature of GJ 229B remains unclear. A 2021 study using data from

A detailed quark level analysis, incorporating the effects of instantons and light gluon exchange, has been conducted to investigate the hadronic spectrum. The study, carried out with a 2+1 lattice configuration of 2.1 TeV mass, yielded results showing that the presence of tetraquark states depends heavily on the interaction mechanisms and quark masses involved. Notably, when the light quark mass is significant, as is the case with the QCD light quarks, the study found no evidence of tetraquark states. Conversely, the lattice data do suggest a signal indicating the presence of a mesic bound state, which could potentially be related to the $f_0(700)$ holed channel.

We will revisit the prediction for $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ within the Standard Model, using its connection to $F_{s}$ through the renormalization group. Our findings align with prior estimates, but with a reduced uncertainty, partly due to a new evaluation of the QCD contributions at the next-to-leading order. We'll also report on the outcome of a worldwide average of $\phi_{s}$ predictions from various analyses within the Standard Model, providing a more precise estimate than previously available. This new average, combined with anticipated improvements in the experimental and theoretical precision in the future, motivates the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

We utilize the aerosol spreading model introduced by Wells and Yang in 2021 to explore the influence of stochastic aerosol dispersal on infection risk. This model builds upon the well-mixed framework by accounting for the spatial movement and removal of aerosol masses. Our analysis expands upon the existing model by incorporating the following key elements: Asymmetric aerosol dispersal, variable air circulation, and aerosol degradation. In order to maintain simplicity, we initially present our results in a two-dimensional setting with specific boundary conditions. Our findings indicate that the well-mixed model yields a satisfactory approximation of the more intricate models within a limited circulation radius but becomes less accurate beyond a certain point as air circulation increases in intensity.

This study delves into the $\gamma$-ray transitions arising from the $\beta$-delayed de-excitation of $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te$^{-}$ isotopes via a combined experimental and theoretical approach. The aim is to derive information about the structure of these even-even nuclei, focusing on their low-lying K$\pi$=$0^-$ states. The $\beta$-decay properties of $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te$^{-}$ were investigated using state-of-the-art $\gamma$-ray detection equipment at the University of Liverpool's Cockcroft Joint Laboratory. The experimental data on $^{137}$Te were supplemented by a full-range gamma-ray linear polarimetry measurement, enabling the determination of the 2$^{+}_1$ state's orientation and alignment. Nuclear shell-model calculations, complemented by a 5-dimensional collective pilot wave method, were performed to describe the calculated $\beta$-decay properties and serve as a reference for the experimental data. The comparison between experiment and theory allows for the validation of the employed nuclear models and the derivation of structure information about the even-even $^{136}$Te nucleus.

This study presents two new sets of uniqueness theorems for exchange programs, along with a detection method for violations that can be automated. Uniqueness theorems for divisors have been established in the past but not in the context of the general exchange program framework. Our new theorems can be applied to instances where the naive preimage might not exist or be computationally impractical to find. A novel algorithm using these theorems enables efficient automatic detection of violations, particularly in large datasets, outperforming previous methods in both speed and scalability.

Our study on the Regge trajectories of light vector mesons, featuring a $F$-wave for the first time, provides mass predictions for the bottom mesons. Utilizing the parameters derived from the light sector, we find the Regge trajectories exhibit a straight trajectory, aligning with other calculations. However, our predictions for the masses of bottom mesons show a systematic deviation from other approaches. Given the significance of the $F$-wave state in various fields like hadronic physics and cosmology, our work provides a framework for its potential utilization in these areas.

We have derived a family of infinite, distinct minimal periodic patterns, which refute Szabados's conjecture in their respective contexts. It's worth noting that for patterns exhibiting less complexity, a different approach can be taken to tackle the conjecture. Our findings indicate that the level of pattern complexity affects the feasibility of different methods to address the conjecture.

A new kernel-based method has been developed to enhance dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), particularly for extracting sparse, nonlinear representations. The approach, called kernel DMD (KDMD), involves applying the kernel trick to data, which enables the identification of low-dimensional patterns through kernel centroids. The authors enhance KDMD by incorporating sparsity, forming a competitive sparse kernel DMD (KS-KDMD) algorithm. They compare the performance of this algorithm with other sparse SPD methods and demonstrate its superior performance in multiple applications.

The evaluation of chess openings and player ability at a professional level has long been a topic of interest in the broader sporting world. To address this, a research approach is outlined, which utilizes a complex dataset comprising a comprehensive collection of chess openings played across various skill levels, from international grandmasters to amateur players. The proposed method employs the Economic Fitness and Complexity algorithm to determine the strategic value of different opening variations and the skill level of players based on their chosen openings. By applying this approach to a large dataset of 16 million rated chess players, the researchers are able to pinpoint specific opening variations that are strongly associated with high player skills and also identify the range of skill levels at which these variations are typically employed.

The Accretion Induced Collapse (AIC) process is a theoretical model that describes the merger of a compact objects, such as neutron stars or white dwarfs in binary systems, which occurs due to gravitational interaction and mass accumulation. It's also possible that stellar collapse could be triggered by a prior binary merger event. Researchers have proposed the concept of a common envelope envelope - a short-lived state that forms when two compact objects orbit each other at close range. Our paper presents a numerical simulation that demonstrates the stability of these systems, using the AMBRE code, a 3D hydrodynamics model that accounts for gravitational and hydrodynamic interactions. Our findings indicate that these systems emit weak jets that don't significantly affect the evolution of the orbit. However, certain variations in the implementation of the equation of state could lead to the emergence of more powerful outflows.

Initially, we establish a method to derive the first integrals of higher-order Euler-Lagrange ODEs, 
noting their correspondence with partial symmetries of the original Lagrangian function. 
Subsequently, we apply this method to the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator and its modified variants, 
thereby confirming a conjecture regarding the non-countable nature of first integrals for this particular model.

Relevant 3D shape retrieval applications often require quick and abstract concept matching between input sketches and target shapes.  Existing sketch-based 3D retrieval methods typically generate image-like representations of sketches and rely on metric learning, but struggle to handle diverse sketch inputs such as abstract concepts, incomplete sketches, and sketches from unseen categories. This research introduces GeoSketches, a 3D sketch retrieval framework that directly maps sketch features to a unified geometric space, allowing for reliable retrieval of shapes even when the target sketch is highly abstract, partially drawn, or from an unseen category. By leveraging a geometric similarity function, GeoSketches outperforms state-of-the-art methods across various 3D sketchbenchmarks and real-world datasets.

HD80606b, a Jupiter-like planet in a 111-day orbit around its star, exhibits an exceptionally unique property: its orbital path causes its spin axis to align perpendicular to the plane of the sky. As a result, the planet experiences a high degree of stellar irradiation during its close approach and virtually no irradiation during its farthest point. Our team utilized the Hubble Space Telescope to monitor the planet's temperature during its close approach in 2016 and 2017. We found that the planet's temperature rose to 1,800K during its close approach and dropped to 600K at its farthest point. Interestingly, we observed a smaller than expected temperature increase due to the planet's thick atmosphere, which absorbs and distributes thermal energy.

Recent computer simulations have suggested that when a certain type of fluid collapses, it may form a finite-point singularity, where the density infinitely compresses at a single point. This point is initially surrounded by a finite region called the "finite-size precursor." This precursor develops even when the fluid doesn't actually form a singularity, by predicting its location based on the fluid's initial mass distribution. We explored the effect of small changes in this mass distribution, such as adding a small, spherical object to the fluid, on the precursor's behavior. Our results show that the singularity's position is accurately predicted even with such small changes, and the precursor's behavior remains nearly unchanged. This implies that the precursor is highly sensitive to even very minor details of the fluid's initial mass distribution.

The weak gravity conjecture suggests that the energy of the lowest lying axion decay mode in a black hole must be greater than or equal to half of the black hole's mass when in a thermal environment. We investigate this idea in the context of three dimensional $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory by considering two canonical ensembles. Our results show that for non-extremal black holes, the condition is satisfied if the state is in thermodynamic equilibrium. For an extremal black hole, the condition is met when the mass of the black hole decreases over time, which indicates that the extremality threshold is crossed. During this process, the rate at which the mass changes must be greater than a certain critical value, which is related to the speed of sound in the theory and the temperature of the thermal state.

Researchers have proposed combining intrinsic and extrinsic methods in reinforcement learning to accelerate training. This study investigates the impact of ground-ed intrinsic motivation, a concept developed by Edwards and Stenning in 1954, when paired with extrinsic rewards in reinforcement learning models. The results show that the inclusion of both ground-ed intrinsic motivation and extrinsic rewards significantly reduces the number of training episodes required by up to 42.9% when compared to using extrinsic rewards alone in the same setting. However, the method of integrating intrinsic and extrinsic motivators has varying effects on training efficiency, with either a positive or negative impact, suggesting that the design of goal sequences is crucial.

We have developed particle model counterparts for both massive and massless versions of colored Poincaré gravity. In order to create these models, we first need to determine the color and Lorentz groups that these particles observe. This is achieved by introducing a new metric that incorporates both the spacetime metric and an internal metric, with subsequent constraints that eliminate unwanted configurations. Following this, the new particle models are formulated through the introduction of covariant fields that meet specific requirements. Particle model interpretations for both massive and massless colored gravitons are provided, with a focus on the latter due to its unique characteristics.

We examine parameterized algorithms for directed acyclic graphs based on their treewidth. Unlike the case with undirected graphs, where treewidth parameterized algorithms are well-established, the equivalent area for directed graphs remains poorly understood. Our study focuses on resolving the $W[+1]$-hardness of Directed Feedback Vertex Set on graphs of bounded treewidth. To address this, we introduce two parameterized algorithms, one for finding a directed feedback vertex set and the other for directed cycle elimination. Our results indicate that both problems can be solved in $f(t)$\cdot n^O(1) time, where $f(t)$ is an increasingly faster function of treewidth. However, we are unable to determine the exact dependence. To better understand the complexity, we also explore cycle detection in directed acyclic graphs and find it to be solvable within reachability time bounds via dynamic programming along tree decomposition.

In the A* algorithm, commonly employed in navigation and related applications, the evaluation function relies on an estimate of goal proximity that is often inaccurate due to its reliance on heuristic information. This has led to the development of more efficient pathfinding methods like MonoHeuristic (MoHe) and MonoLocal (MoLo), which substitute the heuristic with an estimate of goal proximity based on local map information. However, these models have limitations of their own. This study addresses these limitations by combining the strengths of MoHe and MoLo in a multi-layered architecture, named MemoNav. MemoNav is an efficient and robust navigation system that outperforms both A* and its predecessors in a wide range of scenarios.

In the near future, 5G New Radio (5G NR) is being utilized and beyond 5G (5G+) technologies are under development to encompass enhanced wireless services. The unlicensed spectrum band at 6 GHz is gaining attention as a potential additional band for 5G NR and 5G+ to leverage. To support these initiatives, the 3GPP incorporated functionality into Release 16 (Rel-16) to facilitate operation in this band. This paper summarizes the progress made in the Rel-16 standards concerning 6 GHz operation and showcases some demonstrated use cases.

In systems of active particles, long-range interactions and diffusive connections often lead to complex, pattern-forming outcomes. This study examines how these features give rise to spatially diverse and dynamic states in active particle models with global mean-field interactions and shared alignment rules. Through a combination of analytical calculations and numerical simulations, we identify a wide range of heterogeneous states, which are then stabilized by two distinct mechanisms and the influence of one controlling parameter. This mechanism involves either the collapse of fluctuations or the formation of locally active and inactive domains. Depending on the initial conditions, these two processes can result in different stable states. Our findings are further validated by comparing active particle models to an equivalent model of active rods.

The rate at which operators expand in quantum systems can be rigorously calculated 
using the symmetries of the underlying Hamiltonian, thus reducing complex computations.
By employing this method, we have found evidence of slow operator growth in highly entangled many-body states,
including certain instances of fracton and logarithmic Mott insulators.
Additionally, we have applied this approach to determine the impact of symmetry-protected topological ordering 
on physical properties and demonstrated its significance in slow operator growth.
Lastly, we have explored the relationship between topological ordering and the entanglement of low-bond quantum circuits.

The 7.65 MeV state in $^{12}\textrm{C}$, commonly referred to as the Hoyle state, contains a unique 0$^{+}$ subshell structure that is supported by a resonant $^{8}$Be + $\alpha$ pocket. Theoretical models of nuclear decay suggest that this state can be broken down into two primary components: one that follows sequential decay rules and another that doesn't. By analyzing the energy spectra resulting from the decay of this state via the reaction $^{12}\textrm{C}(\gamma, n)$, researchers have discovered new information regarding the non-sequential component. Specifically, a particular 6.18 MeV transition in the energy spectra is indicative of the non-sequential component, and its presence is crucial for understanding the decay process. By factoring in this new information, scientists have revised their previous understanding of the Hoyle state and its internal structure. Interestingly, the calculated widths of the non-sequential component are in line with theoretical models, and these results are expected to further the understanding of this complex nuclear state.

The occurrence of damage in the absence of external damage mechanisms has been extensively researched from a computational and physical perspective. A computational model has been developed that accounts for intrinsic length scales through a non-local formulation, and simulations have been run to model crack propagation in a 2D, pre-stressed brittle material. Through these simulations, it has been found that increased loading speeds can lead to the material overcoming these length scales and entering a zone of stable crack growth, preventing branching and unstable crack propagation. Physically, this has been validated by observing that higher loading rates can shift the stress-strain curve in a way that the material's elastic and plastic responses are altered near the crack tip, promoting a smoother transition from non-linear elastic to plastic deformation.

This study delves into the channel capacity of a memory-affected communication channel, where the receiving end has access to the channel's past state, but not its current or future state. The investigation reveals that increasing the channel's memory capacity ultimately leads to maximal information transmission rates, which grow at a rate proportional to the square root of the number of memory stages, regardless of the channel's state transition probabilities or noise levels. A corresponding decoding algorithm is also proposed, which simulates the channel using neural networks and achieves nearly error-free performance with a large number of memory stages.

In systems combining strong spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity, the superconducting state acquires a topological character through combination with a B-type anti-twisted supercell of the lattice. This topological property arises due to a symmetry-breaking mechanism that forms a topological supercell by folding the superconducting spectrum, similar to how this phenomenon occurs in topological insulators. The resultant topological supercells can be found in various materials with spin-orbit coupling, such as lead and lead alloys, where they feature inherently robust topological properties unaffected by minor adjustments to chemical composition.

In 2021, SEM-TAB-FACTS, a shared task focused on extracting information from sports event summaries, sentences, and tables, was organized in conjunction with the 18th Workshop on Semantics in Acquisition, processing and reasoning. This was done to improve the ability to find relevant data and make accurate inferences from sports commentary by using data from different formats. Four teams took part in the challenge, submitting over 6800 responses across three sub-tasks. The highest overall score was achieved by the System$^2$ team. This paper provides a detailed overview of the task, the data provided, the evaluation metrics, the systems that took part and the results, as well as how to access the data and code.

This paper presents a fundamental explanation of how complex numbers are integral to Quantum Mechanics. We'll begin by examining the essential elements of complex geometry, then explore how they relate to the principles of Quantum Mechanics, specifically highlighting the significance of Hermitian matrices and inner product calculations. By illustrating these concepts with simple examples, we aim to illustrate the necessity of using complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

Consider a finite, connected graph with at least three vertices, where the geodesic distance between pairs of vertices is calculated. A subset of vertices is chosen such that the geodesic distance between every other pair of vertices in the set is accurately determined when the distance is truncated at a certain point. If the minimal cardinality of such a subset is taken for various values of the truncation point, a function $M_{G}(k)$ is obtained, where the minimal value is at most $|\gamma_{G}(k+1)|+1$. In some cases, the minimal value is $|\gamma_{G}(k+1)|$, which happens when the selected vertices have the maximum geodesic distance to each other. When the graph is a complete graph, the function $M_{G}(k)$ can be calculated for any $k$, but it does not match the function $M_{\bar{G}(k)}$ for its complement. If the graph is a tree, its metric dimension can be determined for any $k$, but it does not exceed the number of vertices in the tree. In some cases, the minimal value of $M_{G}(k)$ is less than the number of vertices in the smallest class of the graph.

The steady-state flow equation is a fundamental component of aquifer management, but it is often complicated by varying hydraulic conductivity. By recognizing this, we can transform the full steady-state flow equation into an relevant approximation that accounts for these discrepancies. When hydraulic conductivity is directly proportional to depth, the approximated flow equation differs significantly from the traditional Darcy equation only in the discharge potential gradient equation from near the bottom of the aquifer. Consequently, the approximated equation may provide a more accurate understanding of vertical flow distributions and thus groundwater discharge rates than the traditional Darcy model, especially in situations where hydraulic conductivity is highly depth-dependent.

The study focused on the design and operation of an oxygen-rich, deep-cavity UV-ozone reactor for the removal of sulfur dioxide from flue gases.  The reactor, which features a large reaction zone and long gas residence time, is effective in removing a significant portion of the sulfur dioxide through direct oxidation.  Following initial SO2 oxidation, the resulting sulfur trioxide is further oxidized by excess ozone, resulting in the formation of sulfuric acid, which then condenses into fine droplets, ultimately facilitating the efficient removal of sulfur compounds from the gas phase.  In this study, we examined the design and operational characteristics of such a reactor, as well as the effects of various parameters on its performance, with the ultimate goal of creating a design guideline and a mathematical model that can optimize its operation.  Through our research, we found that a relatively large reactor size and extended residence time are beneficial in achieving high SO2 removal efficiency while also minimizing O3 consumption.  Furthermore, we observed that a relatively small percentage of gas-phase O3 can effectively drive the SO2 oxidation reaction, with the remaining O3 being utilized in the post-oxidation of sulfur trioxide.  However, an increase in temperature or pH value results in a decrease in overall reactor performance, with high temperatures and low pH values being particularly detrimental. Virtual platform-based design allows designers to prototype system architectures without physical prototypes, but segmentation of the virtual platform into different components can significantly impact design speed.  This study examines how various architectures for segmenting virtual platforms into software and hardware components affect simulation speed and also identifies the optimal configuration for achieving this speed improvement.  Our study focuses on a specific application: modeling the latency and throughput of data streams transmitted between different nodes in a neuromorphic architecture.  Using a dataset of 105 examples, we developed a predictive model to determine the optimal configuration for maximum speed.  Our results show that the best architecture for simulating this neuromorphic architecture can achieve a speedup of up to 3.45 times over other possible segmentations while only deviating from the original design in less than 11% on average.

We introduce Indecision Trees, a novel model of probabilistic decision trees that
are capable of representing confidence uncertainties and handling ambiguous input.
These trees can be utilized for classification, regression, and multi-class prediction,
and our algorithm for inducing an Indecision Tree is an adaptation of the well-established
C4.5 method with several modifications to tackle issues that arise from uncertain data.
These problems are commonplace in both real-world and artificial life-like datasets,
where noisy or incomplete data may obscure the underlying patterns in the data set.
Our research aims to address this challenge through the development of robust machine learning algorithms.
Our findings indicate that Indecision Trees exhibit impressive resilience to data irregularities,
outperforming both traditional decision trees and random forests in such scenarios.

Efficiently searching similar time series patterns in large databases is a critical task, commonly required in many real-world applications. The Prism index has emerged as a top-performing solution for this challenge, despite only being adaptable for exact-time series queries. This research aims to extend Prism's applicability by incorporating early abandoning features into the search process, allowing for more query efficiency. The enhanced Prism+AEAB index retains these features and maintains overall search accuracy. The evaluation revealed that Prism+AEAB significantly outperforms even the top-performing general-purpose indexes (e.g., ApproximateRankingIndex) and the optimized Prism index, notably for patterns with lower similarity to database entries (lower tolerance values). The associated code is now available on GitHub under the username @jaimemgon.

We conducted an experiment to examine the impact of giving students access to 
peers' code during a grading process. This study built on previous studies by Chestnut 
and Stewart who studied the effects of various feedback methods in the same setting.
In our research, we investigated the effects of giving students the option to see 
other students' code on multiple dimensions including code coverage, programming 
grades, and what students learned about programming from the experience. The 
underlying hypothesis of the study was that giving students this option would allow 
them to make more informed decisions during the grading process, ultimately leading 
to better outcomes. However, the results of the study indicated that providing this 
opportunity had the opposite effect. When allowed to see peer code, fewer students 
covered all required functions in their code, and their programming grades were 
lower. While students who had access to peer code saw certain benefits in terms of 
what they learned, the benefits of offering this option were largely outweighed by the 
drawbacks for code quality and grades. As such, the study suggests that giving students 
the option to see peer code is not an effective use of instructional resources.

In various contexts, such as the classification of artworks and the detection of medical conditions, decision-making systems that use black-box classifiers are becoming increasingly common. Unfortunately, these systems often lack a clear, interpretable explanation for their decisions, which hinders their adoption and understanding. To address this, we have developed a novel approach that uses properties of the decision-making system to create a simplified, symbolic model, which provides insight into the decision-making process. This symbolic model can be used to identify critical factors and develop new, transparent rules for making classifications, all without requiring access to the underlying model's architecture or the massive dataset used for its training, which can be a significant advantage. We have tested our approach on a powerful, black-box classifier that identifies Attribution-1M image attributes with impressive accuracy, and the results show that the simplified model matches the original's performance while offering crucial insights into its decision-making process.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to identify the root cause to prevent it. This study provides a theoretical explanation for the over-smoothing phenomenon, offering insights into the underlying factors contributing to it. By developing a practical framework to assess the over-smoothing level, researchers can explore various techniques to prevent it. This enables data scientists to select the most effective approach to prevent over-smoothing in their specific use case, rather than relying on general-purpose methods.

We have evaluated the minimum mass thresholds for dark matter particles created during the early universe's inflationary and reheating phases. Our analysis is based on two simplified models, each involving the interaction of a fundamental particle with either a scalar or a vector boson. By restricting the number of possible interactions and the mediator's decay modes, we have established mass threshold limits for dark matter particles. These thresholds are directly related to the ratio of the inflationary and reheating Hubble scales. We have also explored how these thresholds are affected by variations in the decay modes of the mediators and potential non-thermal dark matter initial conditions.

We introduce two new functions of parton virtuality, $sT$ and $sL$, 
to describe parton behavior in the transverse and longitudinal regions, 
respectively, and demonstrate their relationships with previously defined functions, 
$G^Q$ and $H^Q$, as well as $F_1^Q$ and $H_2^Q$, 
and show how these functions can be determined from experimental measurements. 
Notably, the first derivative of $sT$ with respect to parton virtuality is directly linked 
to the parton's transverse motion, while the second derivative is connected to the parton's 
transverse momentum distribution, both at a given scale. Furthermore, the functions 
$sT$ and $sL$ are foundational in describing parton behavior within hadrons and in jets.

This study demonstrates that specific topological spaces, including those derived from products involving the Closed Long Ray and the Long Line with a compact Menger space, exhibit the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property. Additionally, it is proven that a particular type of compactly generated Abelian group, described by suspensions of the integers over the Hilbert cube, cannot display this property when combined with products involving the Compact Cantor Set and the Ordinal Space.

The unique properties of graphene make it an ideal substrate for growing a variety of epitaxial materials, such as Si, GaAs and MoSe2, which exhibit unique properties due to their epitaxial relationship with the substrate. These materials, formed through epitaxial growth on graphene, show enhanced versions of their usual properties and can even be engineered to be lattice-matched, a rare occurrence in traditional material growth. However, the intricacies of graphene's structure pose a challenge to understanding how to control the growth of these new materials, particularly since different graphene domains can develop at varying growth temperatures and result in distinct epitaxial domains with different properties. This research explores how to manipulate graphene's surface to grow high-quality single-crystal moire materials, such as Si, with a specific orientation, by introducing an atomic-scale layer on top of a graphene substrate and adjusting the substrate's atomic arrangement. The findings of this study provide a framework for the precise creation of large-scale single-crystal materials with specific properties.

This study provides an original approach to determining the number of shared stochastic trends between two time series models, featuring a novel estimator. Our analysis indicates that this new estimator is both consistent and efficient, achieving optimal rate of convergence, in the context of finite fourth moments. Notably, under conditions of finite eighth moments or when models have irregular roots, our findings remain accurate with similar convergence rates. The properties of our estimator are also preserved in the presence of heavy-tailed data, where the conventional Johansen approach is compromised. The performance of our estimator is validated through simulated data and in an empirical analysis examining the common trends among key US macroeconomic indicators.

Galaxy cluster lensing observations have provided robust evidence for the cluster's mass, yet the effect of small-mass objects like stars and planetary masses on lensing distortions remains poorly understood. To explore this, researchers have simulated the impact of these small objects in a galaxy cluster and compared the results to strong lensing predictions. Using N-body simulations, they discovered that small objects can induce subtle irregularities in the lensing map, yet their effect on the overall mass distribution and main lensing features remains minimal. By incorporating these small objects into a galaxy cluster model, scientists have found that they can reproduce natural lens systems more effectively than previously estimated. To better comprehend the role of these small objects in galaxy cluster lensing, researchers suggest incorporating them into future weak and strong lensing data analysis to achieve more accurate mass reconstructions and main lens features.

This study examines how network service providers collaborate to offer content from the Internet, with each aiming to maximize their earnings through a combination of investment in quality and negotiation with their peers. Our findings reveal that inter-Internet cooperation encourages content providers to offer incentives in the form of higher payouts to encourage more intense investments by the ISPs, thus resulting in a superior outcome for all parties involved. Contrasting this scenario with a setting where ISPs refrain from cooperating, we identify a substantial disparity in their earnings and investment levels under the cooperative framework.

This article explores the idea of weak naturality in categorical terms, drawing on concepts such as derivable functors and the weakly functorial nature of derived functors in homological algebra. It establishes a derived adjunction framework that incorporates weak naturality and derives the weak naturality of derived functors from any weakly functorial derivable adjunction. Additionally, the article contains a proof that any homological functors for abelian groups are weakly functorial, leading to the conclusion that derived functors preserve natural transformations up to homological equivalence in this specific context.

We have developed a novel exponential $\beta$-attractor model suitable for dark energy cosmology. The exponential model is compared to a polynomial $\beta$-attractor model previously introduced by one of the authors. Both models exhibit similar behavior in their scalar potentials and near their cosmological minimums. To assess their viability, we evaluated their ability to fit observational data from the cosmic microwave background and other sources. Both models were found to provide a good fit to the data, with the exponential model offering a slightly improved fit than the polynomial model in certain aspects. The characteristics of both models, including their near-exponential and near-polynomial behaviors, respectively, contribute to their ability to match the data effectively. The exponential model exhibits a stronger attraction near the minimum, whereas the polynomial model displays a stronger attraction at the intermediate field values. Both models show promise in describing the correct behavior of the universe on cosmological scales.

This study investigates how changing the shape of a filled bending lamination affects the topology of a quasi-Fuchsian 2-dimensional manifold when it's close to its Fuchsian form. We found that there's a one-to-one correspondence between this topological change and a specific type of map that increases the size of the fundamental group of the manifold's boundary while keeping its shape constant.

This study introduces four specialized skewness measures, analogous to those previously established for individual asset returns, but now tailored for use with portfolio data. By differentiating large-capacity investors based on their risk attitudes towards individual and aggregate assets, these new measures help refine existing understanding of portfolio return patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the first four moments of cross-sectional asset returns are interconnected, mirroring the internal relationships observed in individual asset returns. Three specific hypotheses are presented: (1) The Portmom4 measure effectively differentiates between portfolio returns, while also correlating with a generalized version of skewness applicable to portfolio data. (2) The cross-sectional moments of asset returns are interconnected through a dynamic and responsive system. (3) This dynamic system is more pronounced in periods of market stress compared to calm markets, and can be quantified using a measure of market turbulence known as the Stress Index for Portfolio Skewness (SIPS).

Phonocardiogram signal analysis is crucial for cardiac condition diagnosis and monitoring, but it's heavily impacted by background noise, making accurate time-frequency feature extraction and deep model training challenging. This research presents a new end-to-end method utilizing a deep learning approach with a dual mechanism for reducing noise and improving feature extraction. The first mechanism uses a dynamic mask to block noise in the time domain, while the second employs a network that learns to separate the signal and noise in the frequency domain. The proposed method effectively reduces noise and improves feature extraction, ultimately enabling accurate cardiac abnormality detection even in noisy environments, surpassing existing model performances.

A detailed examination of the structural aspects of bi-atomic resonances in green copper acetate and their electric dipole transition properties, occurring at both the molecular and core levels, has been carried out via a combined experimental and theoretical approach. X-ray resonant extended X-ray absorption fine structure (RESXAFS) analysis allowed for a non-destructive investigation of the short-range correlations within the crystals, while density functional theory (DFT) calculations facilitated the extraction of the radial distribution functions. Furthermore, the experimental absorption edges and transition amplitudes were validated by both single-electron and Tamm-Dancoff approximation (TDA) transition state models. Our findings reveal the significant influence of core and tail regions on the transition amplitudes, demonstrating the necessity of considering the entire resonance profile rather than just the main peak.

Let G be a finite group that acts on the real 2-dimensional torus, T^2, in a way that has fixed points. This action can be seen as a twist in a certain sense. We use this twist to establish a connection to the equivariant cohomology with coefficients, specifically examining how the twist affects the generation of the group, G, in the equivariant cohomology ring, H^*(T^2,G)). Our findings show that under the right conditions, the twist can lead to the group, G, being generated by the equivariant cohomology of the 1-skeleton of the torus, when using integer coefficients.

Our research focuses on elevating the social and cooperative aspects within a university's academic department to improve its overall atmosphere. By introducing an online platform that facilitates community building, we aim to increase participant numbers and foster a sense of community among the department's members. This community platform will serve as the foundation for the department's collaborative efforts, featuring a library of shared resources and event scheduling tools to streamline communication and activity organization. To ensure the platform's success, we will conduct extensive outreach to encourage participation and promote the community through a tailored strategy. To gauge the community's progress and member engagement, we will regularly collect and evaluate various metrics. Ultimately, the department's overall atmosphere and the benefits it yields will be assessed through both qualitative and quantitative analyses.

This paper investigates the fractional series operator $T_{\lambda}$ and examines its conditions under which it is bounded from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ into $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. An equivalent characterisation of $T_{\lambda}$'s boundedness is established in relation to the fractional integral operator $I_{\lambda}$, with a subsequent demonstration of its boundedness within a variety of fractional spaces. Furthermore, the article derives the conditions under which $T_{\lambda}$ is bounded from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ into $L^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. With an aim to simplify the calculations, a new equivalent norm for $T_{\lambda}$ is presented on the space $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z}) \cap L^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$.

A type of auction known as the second-price auction is widely regarded as being robust and providing sellers with the highest possible revenue when conducted honestly. However, our study reveals that if sellers engage in non-honest behavior and take risks, they fail to optimize their revenue even when the auction is transparent. We develop a novel model that combines psychological and economic elements to explain why, from a psychological standpoint, non-honest behavior persists despite being detectable. This model highlights two key factors contributing to this phenomenon, namely, the perceived uncertainty associated with punishment and the perceived benefits of deception. Our study offers a framework that bridges the gap between these two perspectives, yielding a unique prediction regarding how this auction plays out in the presence of uncertainty and risk aversion. To test these predictions, we conducted an online experiment featuring second-price auctions, with results supporting our theoretical claims. Specifically, our study finds that sellers do not always strive to maximize their revenue, instead sometimes offering lower prices in an attempt to deceive buyers. Moreover, we observe that the level of risk aversion and uncertainty associated with uncertainty and punishment affect how often and to what extent sellers cheat. Notably, our study reveals that sellers tend to engage in more deception when the level of risk aversion is higher and when the likelihood of uncertainty is higher, while also detecting an interaction between these factors that impacts revenue optimization.

We're investigating how the universe's anisotropic characteristics influence its own evolution. Initially, this investigation assumes the universe starts off in an extremely complex and dynamic state, which however simplifies over time as it becomes increasingly isotropic, a common pattern, much like a spinning top losing its wobble as it approaches equilibrium. A specific anisotropic cosmological model is being examined in this study, which is based on a complex metric with two distinct scale factors representing space and time dimensions. Following the introduction of a complex Ricci tensor, which incorporates both the Ricci and the complex scalar field's interactions, the model's validity is being validated through the Big Bang Singularity Theorem. A subsequent analysis of the universe's dynamics, particularly its scalar factor, indicates that it exhibits a universal contraction, a characteristic contraction, during the early stages, which however gives way to an isotropic expansion as the universe progresses. A rough estimate of the universe's age at which this transition occurs is being calculated in this study.

This research explores Gr\"obner fan and Gr\"obner fan-type decomposition for a specific type of variety, known as Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on the region characterized by a maximal value of $t$. The Gr\"obner fan of an ideal is a geometric representation of the various Gr\"obner bases associated with a combinatorial model, and it can be applied to local regions of this variety, parametrized by a vector of values, $t$. A Gr\"obner fan-type decomposition of an ideal occurs when the associated variety can be broken down into disjoint regions, each corresponding to a unique Gr\"obner basis. Building on previous work of Bigas and Oeding for certain regular subvarieties of $SL_2$, this study computes the Gr\"obner fan and finds a Gr\"obner fan-type decomposition for the local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties for specific combinatorial configurations and higher rank cases, while also proving that no such decomposition exists for others.

This paper introduces a innovative approach to generating high-quality brushstrokes for art, utilizing a novel stroke synthesis model based on GANs. We've developed a groundbreaking stroke generation algorithm, enabling the creation of novel brushstrokes from a single image, as well as multiple styles from a single sample. Furthermore, our approach has been successfully applied to the generation of painted textures, yielding impressive results in the domain of AI art.

We synthesize current knowledge of flavor anomalies within $K$ and $B$ meson systems, focusing particularly on the relationship between lepton-flavor universality and these anomalies.
